#3191. Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pros may be late, but they have one big advantage

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple finally revealed its new MacBook M5 Pro and Max with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing the best features from the iPhone to its laptops.

Steve Jobs might be rolling over in his grave, but at long last, Apple announced a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen display. The new MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max features a tandem OLED display Apple is calling “ProLED XDR”, scaling up to 2,000 nits of brightness and a 120Hz refresh rate. For the first time, the MacBook Pro will feature touchscreen capabilities and the Dynamic Island — a feature first introduced on the iPhone.

Also: Forget the touchscreen MacBook – Apple’s new M6 is the laptop I recommend for most people

The display and controversial form factor aren’t its only draws: it features a thinner, lighter design and brings back the illuminated Apple logo on the back — some of the most significant changes to the MacBook chassis in years. The new MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips will come in both 14- and 16-inch sizes, with up to 128GB of unified memory, and weigh less than ever: the smaller model at three pounds and the 16-inch at four pounds.

The company, under new CEO John Ternus, is on a spree with new products, with its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, earlier this month (another product that’s been in development for years), and an all-new lineup of smart home products aimed at challenging Amazon’s dominance in that market.

The MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max feature new ProLED XDR displays that control color and pixel luminance at the sub-millisecond level, while monitoring and adapting usage over time, Apple says. The panels feature a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and cover both the P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts, high-end specs indeed for a laptop display.

To reduce glare, Apple says it etched the nano-texture directly into the glass, since the touch sensor is built directly into the panel rather than layered on top of it.

The displays work with Apple’s ProMotion technology, which adjusts refresh rates based on what the device is actively doing: scaling down to 10Hz while idle for better power efficiency and ramping up to 120Hz during gaming or graphics-heavy tasks.

In terms of software and usability, Apple says apps should be ready to go on the new MacBook Pros, since they’re set to register touches as clicks.

Touchscreen laptops are nothing new, having been standard fare on laptops of all kinds for years now. Apple’s entrance into the market is notable because the company took such a hard-line stance against them for years (Jobs famously called them “ergonomically terrible“), but honestly, the everyday consumer in 2026 may struggle to see the big deal.

Either you like using your finger or a stylus on a screen, or you don’t. Can Apple really deliver a touchscreen experience that is worlds better than what’s available on Windows PCs or Chromebooks (or Googlebooks)? It’s debatable.

However, there are a few things Apple has up its sleeve that set it apart from the competition, and they have to do with its most successful product of all time (which also happens to have a touchscreen): the iPhone.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: The $2,000 foldable has some magical touches

Apple smartly made the iPhone’s usability wins core to its approach to the new MacBook. For example, it features a Dynamic Island cutout, doing away with the notch in favor of a dynamic multitasking hub. This allows it to adapt through unique touch-based interactions that were previously impossible on a MacBook.

The Dynamic Island serves as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri, changing how you interact with these features by putting them front and center. The design intent here appears to be to keep dynamic, time-sensitive events and apps in close view for quick reference, an interesting merge of how we use both our iPhones and laptops.

Also: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook is days away – with another OLED surprise

Plus, with Apple’s vast App Store library, there is already a host of touch-optimized programs for Apple’s ecosystem. It doesn’t look like Apple is interested in bringing these directly to MacOS — this is still very much a MacBook Pro — instead, folding in the touch functionality as part of the feature set of these laptops’ premium displays.

In that sense, this is already well-trodden ground for Apple. Bringing the best features of the iPhone to the MacBook Pro isn’t even that revolutionary when you think about it; it’s a smart way to improve its product line.

You already know these new MacBooks aren’t going to be cheap. The base model with the lowest configuration starts at $2,899: the 14-inch M5 Pro with 24GB of unified memory and 1TB of local storage. The prices only scale up from there to seriously astronomical figures, particularly for the ultra-high-end storage options. 16TB of storage will start at $14 grand.

We haven’t seen these laptops in person yet, but I have no doubt the new ProLED XDR screens look fantastic. However, it’s a lot of money for a touchscreen laptop. These devices come hot on the heels of Microsoft and Nvidia’s recent RTX Spark devices, which also target the high end of the market, with AI enthusiasts looking for local AI performance to be front and center.

These laptops are niche, to be sure, but they also don’t speak to such a specific subset of users; instead, they focus on their impressive hardware and implications for creators, artists, and power users.

Also: Apple’s touchscreen Mac event: 3 things I’m excited for – and my one concern

Apple isn’t showcasing a reinvention of the MacBook Pro, but rather a bonus feature for its most powerful ultra-premium laptops. With the recent announcement of the M6 MacBook Pro, consumers looking for an accessible workhorse MacBook already have that option. This is for someone else entirely.

The new MacBook Pros with M5 Pro and M5 Max are now available for preorder, with general availability beginning Friday, Nov. 6.

#3190. John Ternus addresses iPhone Duo supply constraints, display issue

Today Apple reported record Q4 earnings, which beat Wall Street expectations overall. And in an interview with Reuters, CEO John Ternus addressed current iPhone Duo supply constraints and also referenced units that have been returned for display issues.

Apple’s latest quarterly earnings did not include any sales for the iPhone Duo. That’s because it covered a period running July-September, and the Duo didn’t go on sale until October.

But Wall Street is understandably still very curious about how sales for the foldable are going. Especially as relates to revenue forecasts for the current quarter.

In an interview with Reuters, Ternus addressed two aspects of the iPhone Duo: supply constraints and units that have had display issues.

Regarding supply, it sounds like Apple doesn’t know when it might reach supply-demand balance:

“Duo is constrained as of today,” Ternus said. “The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we’re not ‌able to ⁠predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Currently, shipping estimates from the Apple Store are still set for late January. That’s where they’ve stayed since the first pre-orders immediately sold out on October 16.

On the matter of iPhone Duo screens cracking, Ternus was brief and essentially repeated what Apple had previously confirmed: that the issue is real, but limited to a very small number of units.

Ternus told Reuters that “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duo units had been returned with display issues. Apple is replacing those units with new models.

#3188. The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

From a new smart alarm clock to an Alexa-powered 3D map of your home, here's what's new from Amazon, including prices and release dates.

Amazon announced several new smart home devices today, including two all-new device categories: the $200 Echo Time smart alarm clock and the $230 Alexa Photo Frame. Both are available now, along with an upgraded Echo Dot for $100 and a new Echo Studio with a built-in Home Camera for $250.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

The company’s smart home lineup also now includes a redesigned $500 Echo Show 16, which is available for preorder, with devices shipping in mid-December. Finally, Amazon announced the Alexa Home Map, which lets you create a 3D interactive map of your home’s interior and exterior.

Here are all the biggest updates to know.

The Amazon Echo Time is a new bedside companion and a definite upgrade over the Echo Spot. It’s a rounded speaker with a display and no camera, designed to be the smartest combination of alarm clock and hub available.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

The Echo Time doubles as a smart home hub, since it supports Zigbee and Matter and acts as a Thread border router. It costs $200, so it’s a definite price hike compared to the Echo Spot, but it’s also a more capable speaker with hub capabilities.

The Amazon Alexa Photo Frame is another first for Amazon, arriving just in time for the holidays. The photo frame consists of a 10.1-inch matte display with Alexa+ built in, made to cycle through your own collection of photos. It also allows you to search for specific photos by voice, as well as record voice notes associated with individual photos.

The Alexa Photo Frame comes in three frame finishes, including Birch, Walnut, and Black, so it can fit in with your home decor. It costs $230 and is already available for purchase.

Amazon also announced some big upgrades coming to the Echo lineup. They include a redesigned Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and an upgraded Echo Studio with Home Camera.

The new Alexa Home Map lets you create a 3D interactive map of your home’s interior and exterior, allowing you to navigate floors, zoom into rooms, and see the locations of all your devices while controlling them in real time.

The concept isn’t a novel idea for Amazon, but the Alexa Home Map elevates the experience offered by the Amazon Alexa app’s Map View feature, which we covered at launch three years ago. Map View lets you create a basic layout of the rooms inside your home to place and tap device icons.

Unlike Map View, which focuses on indoor smart devices within four walls, the new Alexa Home Map offers a 360-degree aerial view of your property. It uses your Ring cameras to generate animations of people and cars moving around your yard and uses the controversial Familiar Faces feature to let you know who was detected.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets

You create the 3D interactive map of your home by using a compatible smartphone with a lidar feature to scan each room and then putting them together. You can then place Alexa-compatible smart home devices in each room and interact with them in real time, like turning on a light or lowering the volume on a speaker.

For the exterior of your home, enter your address, and the app will generate an Alexa Home Map of your residence using existing map data.

Using integrations with compatible Alexa devices, including Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV devices, and other “Works with Alexa” smart home devices, will improve your home security, Amazon says. But it also opens the door for a whole lot more surveillance of your home, both for potential bad actors and for Amazon itself.

Amazon claims that the Alexa Home Map will update dynamically in real time, gathering data from your smart devices in and around your home. As a result, it can show the color of your smart twinkle lights during the holidays, as well as animations of people and cars moving around your property.

A vulnerability in a single third-party smart device could theoretically be used to pivot deeper into your home network or manipulate the map interface, not to mention that the data in this 3D map will include sensitive and private behavioral patterns, like when the family leaves the home or when children return.

Also: Kindle Colorsoft review: My favorite color e-reader just got better with this thoughtful upgrade

#3187. Apple spent a record $45.77 billion on R&D in fiscal 2026, up 32%

Apple’s research and development expenses reached a new all-time high in fiscal 2026, climbing 32% year over year to $45.77 billion. Here are the details.

While it may have taken Apple longer than some wished it had to ramp up R&D in the face of growing competition in AI, the company has significantly accelerated its spending over the past year.

As Apple shared in its Q4 2026 results, it spent $11.73 billion on R&D, bringing its total spending for fiscal 2026 to $45.77 billion, a 32% increase compared to the $34.55 billion it spent in fiscal 2025.

During an earnings call earlier this year, former CEO Tim Cook said Apple was “clearly investing more,” adding that R&D was “accelerating much higher than the company” overall. CFO Kevan Parekh also explained that AI-related spending was being added to the investments Apple was already making in its existing product roadmap.

Interestingly, today’s figures also suggest that Apple’s R&D spending may be starting to level off.

While Apple’s Q4 2026 R&D expenses were up 32% from $8.87 billion in the year-ago quarter, they were virtually unchanged from Q3, increasing by just $1 million. As the chart above shows, Apple’s R&D spending jumped significantly at the beginning of fiscal 2026, but has since stabilized at a much higher level than in previous years.

The iPad mini 8 is releasing later this week, and we're excited to see what this new pint-sized Apple tablet can do. However, some of you may be wondering what happened to all the other iPads that are due for refreshes. Well, it turns out they may be arriving in early 2027.

This comes from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, who claims that Apple will release three new iPads in the first half of 2027. The lineup includes an upgraded low-end tablet, the iPad 12, an OLED iPad Air, and a more powerful version of the iPad Pro.

The release of the iPad Air is not a huge surprise, considering new versions of that particular tablet tend to arrive in the first half of the year anyway. The iPad 12 has been long-rumored to come with an A19 or A18 chipset, alongside an increased 8GB of RAM. This means it'll be able to run Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, though some of the more advanced on-device features will still be out of reach. It's still going to be an entry-level device, though, so we shouldn't expect any significant upgrades like an OLED display, or possibly even 256GB of base storage. #3185. Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding, ranking alongside Codex GPT-6.1 Terra

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Mistral has released the weights for Large 4, along with some impressive Artificial Analysis scores.

French AI lab Mistral shipped its latest model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk” for its trillion-parameter size, in preview on Oct. 6. As promised, the lab has released the model’s weights, alongside some new benchmark scores that show Western open models gaining ground over their Chinese peers.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

After three weeks of testing with a select group of partners, Mistral’s model sets a new standard for Western-made open models, ranking at the top of Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index among open models globally. The model also comes with three reasoning modes now (low, medium, and high), as is common for heftier models to give users more options based on their level of task complexity.

ML4’s score on the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped to 41% from its preview version’s 28% to 41%, beating Opencode’s GLM-5.3 by one small but important point. On the overall Index, however, which shows a model’s composite score across three relevant benchmarks, ML4 is a point behind GLM-5.3, scoring a 48 to GLM-5.3’s 49. Codex GPT-6.1 Terra also scores a 48 overall.

As a reminder, benchmark scores themselves should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering how many models cheat.

Still, that improvement in performance is meaningful for just a few weeks of extra training. As proprietary AI remains expensive to use, economical models that don’t sacrifice performance are eye-catching. ML4 “rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% less tokens per task on average,” Mistral said.

When Mistral released ML4 in preview earlier this month, it touted how the model prioritizes cyber defense capabilities, advertising customizable control and data sovereignty. The company has spent the last few weeks working with developers and leaders to assess the model’s cybersecurity capabilities, a practice that’s becoming commonplace for proprietary American labs like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic as concerns about model security mounts.

Similarly to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s rollout of Astra, Mistral’s initial testing partners got access to a less guardrailed version of ML4 with “expanded cybersecurity capabilities.”

At least by some measure, ML4’s promises seem to have come true: Le Chonk scored just above DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the CyberGym benchmark for defensive cybersecurity, which measures how well models find “real memory-safety vulnerabilities in C/C++ open-source projects, reproducing them with proof-of-concept inputs, and patching them without breaking the projects’ tests.”

Recent AI security incidents have somewhat pitted open and proprietary models against each other. Initially framed as less safe because of their malleability, open models are viewed as a new option for cyber defense after proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI proved just as risky.

Mistral said ML4 is built for security that stays under user control — unlike proprietary models, which frontier labs can technically rescind access to at any time.

“The cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample said during a briefing for the Oct. 6 preview release.

Following the Hugging Face breach, Mistral was one of many companies that signed Nvidia’s Open Secure AI Alliance, a cross-industry partnership that argues open models are crucial to democratizing defenses against increasingly common AI security incidents.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware

By Nvidia’s logic, and its Alliance that aims to democratize AI security tools, the race is between Mistral and other open models to achieve state-of-the-art security prowess.

Training a competitive model in a compute shortage is no small task for a trimmer lab like Mistral, which doesn’t have the same resources as a pre-IPO giant like Anthropic.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“ML4 was trained from scratch on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months, deployed in Mistral’s own data centers in Europe,” the company said. For context, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said on X that OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on roughly 100,000 GPUs.

#3181. Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined – update both ASAP

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The latest version of Firefox fixes 167 security vulnerabilities, most of which are of high severity, while the newest version of Chrome patches 52 flaws, four of which are critical.

With security vulnerabilities continually plaguing the software we use, it’s time once again to update both Firefox and Chrome browsers to protect yourself from the latest exploits.

Also: Half of all cyberattacks start in your browser: 10 tips for staying safe

This week, Mozilla updated Firefox to version 159, not just for Windows but also for Android, MacOS, and Linux. The latest version includes fixes for 167 security bugs. Among these, 108 are rated of high severity, while the rest are considered moderate or low.

Almost 100 of them are defined as use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, which are memory management flaws that an attacker could exploit to crash the browser or trigger malicious code. Several of the bugs also refer to Firefox’s Sandbox, which means that hackers could break through the browser’s protected Sandbox area to execute malicious code.

Given the nastiness of the security bugs, you’ll want to update Firefox ASAP. For that, open the browser, click the three-line icon at the upper right, move to Help and Report, and select About Firefox. The latest update will then be installed. Restart Firefox to finish the process.

Also: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back

Beyond the security patches, Firefox 159 adds a few handy new features.

With Firefox for the Mac, sharing a page in the browser now displays the built-in MacOS share picker. Here, you can see a preview of the page you want to share along with recent contacts and specific apps such as AirDrop and Messages.

Next up, you’re now able to access Firefox’s passwords tool in the sidebar. This lets you more easily view any website passwords that you’ve saved to the browser. To see this in action, first make sure the sidebar is visible. For that, click the Sidebar button on the Address bar and then click the key icon to display your saved passwords.

And as perhaps the most helpful new feature, Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window can now watch specific web pages for changes and send you a notification when the page is updated. For this, turn on the option for Smart Window if it’s not already enabled. Click the Firefox icon in the upper right and select Smart Window. Navigate to the website for which you’d like to be notified of any changes. At the chat window, type /watch, fill out the form, and then click the Create Task button.

That takes us to Chrome with version 56.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux. Here, the latest update patches 52 security bugs. Out of these, four are rated critical, while 46 are rated high.

The four severe ones point to a memory corruption problem. But like some of the Firefox bugs, they also reference the browser’s Sandbox. In this case, an attacker who exploits any of these vulnerabilities could bypass Chrome’s protected Sandbox area to run malicious code. Also as in Firefox, several of the bugs point to use-after-free (UAF) issues that would allow an attacker to exploit memory management flaws to crash the browser or install malicious code.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

To update Chrome, click the three-dot icon at the top, move to Help, and select About Google Chrome. If prompted, allow the latest update to download and then restart the browser to finish.

Beyond many of the bugs themselves, Firefox and Chrome also share an increasing reliance on AI to find and resolve security flaws. In its advisory, Mozilla cited Amy Burnett, a security research and analyst at OpenAI, for uncovering many of the bugs. In its blog post, Google attributed the discovery of several flaws to Anthropic’s Claude and a few to OpenAI.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3180. Apple says memory costs and Siri AI will weigh on holiday quarter profit margins

Following today’s earnings report, Apple held its quarterly earnings call, during which the company discussed the impact of rising memory costs on its profit margins and warned of additional pressure from Siri AI expenses during the holiday quarter. Here are the details.

Over the past few quarters, Apple has repeatedly warned that rising component costs would put pressure on its profit margins. Last quarter, gross margin was 50.1%, up from 49.3% in Q2. However, that included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.

Today, Apple reported that its gross margin fell to 47.9% in Q4 2026, with product gross margin dropping to 37.2%, down from 40.1% in the previous quarter. That represented a 2.2-percentage-point decline in company-wide gross margin and a 2.9-percentage-point drop in product gross margin.

Against the backdrop of record September quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh explained that tariff refunds once again provided some relief, though not enough to offset the impact of rising memory costs. He also noted that, excluding the impact of tariff refunds, the sequential decline in gross margins would have been roughly one percentage point, primarily due to higher memory costs:

“We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs.”

Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon, with the company forecasting gross margins of between 45% and 46% for Q1 2027.

He attributed the expected decline primarily to higher memory costs, alongside the impact of the ongoing Siri AI rollout.

When asked to elaborate, Parekh explained that Siri AI will affect Apple’s margins in two ways. First, running the service will increase cloud costs. Second, Apple will have to spread out the recognition of some revenue from devices that include Siri AI over their lifetimes, rather than counting it all at the time of sale.

This, he added, is an accounting practice Apple already follows for other services bundled with its devices, such as Maps, Siri, and iCloud:

“Consistent with how we’ve always accounted for Maps, Siri, and iCloud, for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device.”

Meanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter.

Ternus said recent price increases across the Mac, iPad, and iPhone lineups would help offset some of those costs, alongside existing inventory purchased at lower prices and savings on certain non-memory components. He also warned that the benefits of carrying lower-cost memory inventory would diminish over time. Apple did not say whether it expects to raise product prices yet again to compensate.

#3179. Your headphones have hidden LE Audio features you’ll want to know about

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Your JBL, Sony, or Bose Bluetooth headphones got a top-to-bottom wireless makeover -- not just Auracast.

The shift from Classic Bluetooth to LE Audio is in full swing, as JBL and Sony release flagship headphones and earbuds with built-in LE Audio. Bose is the latest to upgrade its flagship headphones via an OTA firmware update.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Auracast, the Bluetooth protocol that enables one-to-many audio streams and is the most popular LE Audio feature, but several other LE Audio upgrades don’t get as much attention. These features improve wireless voice call quality, reduce battery drain in true wireless earbuds, and remove ecosystem barriers to low-latency mobile gaming. Here’s why they matter just as much as Auracast.

LE Audio includes the Low Complexity Communication Codec (LC3), which includes the unified Telephony and Media Audio Profile (TMAP) to handle audio streams and voice calls simultaneously. Bluetooth Classic relies on the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile (A2DP) and Hands-Free Profile (HFP), which handle the same functions but require both profiles.

Also: Bluetooth’s latest could solve a common connectivity problem

The profiles in Bluetooth Classic, given that they must alternate, result in extremely poor voice quality during hands-free calls over cellular or video calls on Zoom or Teams. These profiles also account for degraded voice quality when chatting while playing a mobile game.

LE Audio consolidates these two profiles, creating higher-quality, bidirectional audio and preserving voice call quality when using wireless headphones.

Earlier this year, JBL gave its flagship Tour Pro 3 earbuds an OTA firmware update to support LE Audio, and Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds, released in February, have LE Audio support out of the box. There’s one major true wireless earbud improvement wrapped in LE Audio: native multi-stream audio.

Also: Frustrated with multipoint? How it works – and why it sometimes won’t

In Bluetooth Classic, your source device, such as your phone, sends audio to one earbud, which then retransmits it to the other earbud. This complex audio transmission method is why one of your earbuds always has a lower battery than the other. Though premium earbuds usually have an independent stream workaround, many midrange and budget earbuds don’t, and that’s where LE Audio comes in handy.

LE Audio enables independent audio streams built into the Bluetooth stack, so manufacturers don’t need to implement their own methods to avoid asymmetrical battery drain.

Software ecosystems, like Apple’s iOS and Samsung’s Galaxy, dictate which audio features are reserved for devices inside of them and withhold features from devices outside of them. Hardware ecosystems are equally responsible for the fragmentation of audio features across manufacturers, typically through codecs.

Sony’s LDAC codec for high-quality audio is only available on Sony headphones, earbuds, and smartphones with the proper hardware, which is limited in the US market. Snapdragon’s AptX codecs aren’t as widely available on phones either, leaving most people to rely on Bluetooth Classic SBC and AAC codes, even though their headphones support more advanced ones.

Also: Your iPhone may support Bluetooth Channel Sounding – and it’s a big deal

LE Audio eliminates the tedious codec issue, especially in wireless gaming contexts, delivering lower latency, improved voice audio streams, and eliminating asymmetrical audio transmission.

For now, as long as you have a compatible Android phone, you have access to several models of headphones, earbuds, and Bluetooth speakers that support LE Audio. As more manufacturers update their devices to support the Bluetooth audio streaming protocol, this suggests the technology is becoming more reliable.

So, what about your AirPods? I wouldn’t bet on it anytime soon.

Late last week, a report popped up about a new Android phone exploit the security researcher dubbed "SMS of Death." Per the report, the attack, tracked as "CVE-2026-58882," lets malicious actors disrupt cellphone service or crash Android phones by overloading them with a repeating crafted SMS text message.

The denial-of-service flaw can even interrupt ongoing calls, including emergency calls, without requiring you to open the message. Apparently, the Android operating system processes the message before it even reaches your text message inbox, meaning you wouldn't immediately understand what caused the phone to crash.

Researcher Mark Blah says that even if you reboot your phone, the hacked message "stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below)."

Upon finding Blah's report, Tom's Guide reached out to Google because the report claimed that Google had deemed it a "non-priority." Google has not yet responded to our inquiries.

However, some Android phones may already have the exploit patched.

Blah's report found that the exploit affects Android versions 12 up to 16 and was discovered on multiple devices, including Pixel 9s and Samsung Galaxy phones.

It appears Google patched the exploit in the October 2026 Android security update (if you haven't updated your Android phone, you should). However, that's only for Android versions 14 through 17. It does not appear to be available for any devices still running Android 12 or 13.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Per Blah, the flaw uses an improper validation of a header length in the Android WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu function. Attacks send a malformed WAP Push message to the targeted phone.

When this message is translated, it turns into a negative value that Android attempts to allocate memory for, which triggers a NegativeArraySizeException that crashes the com.android.phone process.

That process manages cellular functions, which disrupts connectivity and disconnects calls. This causes repeated crashes because the network tries to redeliver the malicious messages, which stack up and force Android to process each one. It only takes 20 bad messages to cause the crash.

Per the Google fix, the crash is prevented by catching the exceptions triggered by the attack messages. Then the patch deletes the messages from the SMS database to prevent them from looping.

Android security updates are generally automatically installed on supported devices. So you should already have them.

However, availability does depend on the phone maker and network carrier. So you should check your phone to see if the October patch has been applied. A restart may be required to complete the installation.

For the most part, this isn't an attack you can do anything about, but based on the patch notes and Blah's report, it doesn't seem to be widely deployed; instead, it appears to target individual phones. Since a working proof-of-concept of the exploit has been released, the best thing you can do is make sure you keep your phone up to date.

There's something new on the ballot this time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI data centers are powering everything from ChatGPT to Google's Gemini, but the enormous facilities that make these tools possible are facing growing resistance across the country.

On Tuesday, November 3, voters in 10 states will decide on 41 local ballot measures involving data centers, according to Ballotpedia. Twenty-eight measures would restrict development if approved, while 13 would make it easier for projects to move forward.

The votes come as Americans face rising electricity costs and questions about how much power AI infrastructure should consume, who pays for new energy infrastructure and whether communities benefit enough from having these facilities nearby.

For households already struggling with higher utility bills, the debate has become about more than where technology companies build their next server farms.

Data centers are essential to the AI boom. They power cloud storage, streaming services, internet applications and the sophisticated AI systems used by millions of people every day.

But they also require enormous amounts of electricity to operate servers and cooling systems around the clock. A June 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, with projections ranging from 9.5% to 15.3%.

That growing demand is putting pressure on utilities to expand generating capacity, transmission lines and other infrastructure.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

And consumers are growing concerned about whether they'll be asked to help pay for those upgrades.

According to Reuters, residential electricity prices have increased more than 10% nationally since 2024, with increases exceeding 20% in Ohio.

Not every increase can be attributed to data centers. Rising fuel costs, aging infrastructure and other factors also contribute. But rapid growth in electricity demand is raising questions about how utilities allocate costs between large commercial customers and existing households.

Ohio is at the center of the debate. According to Ballotpedia, the state accounts for 21 of the 41 measures appearing on November 3 ballots.

Several communities, including Sunbury, Defiance and Oregon, will vote on proposals to prohibit data centers that consume more than 25 megawatts of electricity.

In Sunbury, the restrictions could affect a proposed $2 billion Amazon data center project, according to Reuters. But the issue goes well beyond Ohio. California, voters in Alhambra will decide whether to prohibit data centers within city limits. In Edgewater, Florida, residents will consider an amendment restricting new data center development and expansion.

Several Maine communities will vote on temporary moratoriums, potentially pausing projects while local officials establish development rules.

In Illinois, some voters will will weigh advisory questions about whether their communities should support or restrict data center construction.

And in New Jersey, residents of Downe Township will answer a straightforward question: Do they support data centers in their community? The New Jersey vote is advisory, meaning it measures public sentiment rather than directly authorizing or prohibiting construction.

The measures across the country differ significantly. Some establish outright bans, others would restrict only the largest facilities, and some would impose additional approval requirements. The common thread for all is that more communities want a greater say in how AI infrastructure is built.

Electricity markets operate across large regions, meaning power demand in one community can affect costs well beyond its borders. The PJM regional electricity market, for example, serves New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia and other states. According to a recent FactCheck.org analysis, PJM's independent market monitor has identified data centers as a primary driver of higher capacity market prices.

The monitor estimates that data center demand will add billions of dollars in capacity market charges over the current and following delivery years.

Those charges are shared across the regional electricity market, although the impact on individual household bills varies. Even if a community blocks a new facility, demand from AI companies could shift to another location. Existing infrastructure costs and broader electricity-market conditions would remain.

Likewise, approving a project doesn't automatically mean household bills will increase. The outcome depends partly on whether utilities and regulators require developers to cover the infrastructure costs their facilities create.

Technology companies and development supporters argue that data centers create construction jobs, generate tax revenue and attract investment.Amazon, which has major expansion plans in Ohio, has emphasized the employment opportunities, economic benefits and technology services associated with its facilities.

Supporters also argue that data centers are necessary to support the digital services that households and businesses depend on, including AI tools that are rapidly becoming part of everyday life.

Restrictions, they warn, could move those investments to communities with more favorable development policies.

Opponents raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, noise, land use and the possibility of households subsidizing infrastructure built primarily for large technology companies. The issue crosses traditional political lines, with local opposition emerging in communities across the country.

Tomorrow's election results could affect where major technology companies build new data centers, how local governments regulate them and the conditions developers must meet before construction begins.

For consumers in the U.S., tomorrow may determine how communities and utility regulators will manage the growing electricity and infrastructure demands of AI without placing unnecessary costs on existing customers.

Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday.

Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt.

"Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington.

"The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery."

Murphy, who came to the Senate in 2013, is not up for reelection on Tuesday, but he's been crisscrossing the country campaigning for Democratic candidates, with recent stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He was due in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas.

He's seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and is a prolific Democratic fundraiser.

Murphy, 53, spent six years in the House before running for the Senate. He rose to national prominence as an advocate for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting, which occurred in his home state. He's been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has opposed the war in Iran and the White House's deportation policies.

He's one of multiple sitting senators to suffer a stroke in recent years.

Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland each had a stroke in 2022. And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., who was then running for office, suffered a stroke just days before his state's Senate Democratic primary.

"Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy. I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a fellow Connecticut Democrat, posted to X on Sunday.

#3170. Android 17 adoption hits a staggering 1% – why you really should update now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Only a quarter of Android phones have even made it to Android 16.

Android 17 adoption hasn’t been speedy. According to the most recent data from heise.de via Android Studio, as reported by Android Authority, Android 17 has reached just 1% of active devices since its release in June 2026.

While Android 16 is finally the most used Google OS for Android devices, at 25.4% of active Android devices, these distribution figures indicate that getting users to upgrade to even newer software is an uphill battle.

It’s true that Android 17 has had less time to reach devices than Android 16 did when the previous distribution snapshot was published, but the minuscule adoption rate underscores how slowly the latest release is infiltrating the Android ecosystem.

Also: How Android 17 stops network snoops and SMS blasters now

Plus, the data show that more Android users than not are running versions that are many years old. I’m all for not fixing what’s not broken, but when Android 14 is the second most widely used version (15.% of devices are still running it), while Android 15 trails not far behind at 14.7%, there’s a pretty large chunk of individuals who may be putting themselves (and their data) at risk.

And it doesn’t end there. Android 13 and Android 11 are still on the table for 11.8% and 10.1% of users, with almost another 10% still using Android 12. That’s about another 30% of users still running Android 13 or older.

Though the numbers indicate that almost 60% of active Android devices are running Android 14 or newer, about 40% of users haven’t even upgraded to Android 14 or later.

Also: This Android 17 setting logs suspicious activity on your phone for troubleshooting

While the numbers are staggering, they’re not surprising. Android updates typically lag behind iOS updates. While the iPhone and its software are both designed, controlled, and distributed by Apple, Android updates must roll out from a single starting point to a wider array of mobile devices and systems to reach users. While Google is responsible for the core of the Android system, those updates must then be curated, reviewed, and pushed to every device that uses Android. This includes phones from Google, Samsung, Nothing, and more, which usually requires adaptations from each manufacturer. Apple’s updates are often adopted faster because there’s no middle entity between iOS and the user, while Android’s process is rather fragmented.

Keep in mind that Google no longer publishes a regularly updated public distribution chart, so this data isn’t from a real-time survey of every Android device. There’s only cumulative adoption data through Android Studio, and these estimates are derived from those figures and cover devices that contacted the Google Play Store during a seven-day period.

It’s always good practice to keep your device updated to the latest available software that your system allows. There are a few great reasons why those eligible for Android 17 should upgrade, including improved features — like the ability to “bubble” apps and stop network snoops and SMS blasters.

Also: I enabled Android’s new security feature that detects fake cell towers – here’s why

Plus, it’s the most proactive thing you can do for your device. Software updates usually include improvements to your phone’s operation, speed, security, and more, and it’s an easy (and free) way to keep your phone healthy.

#3168. Amazon (AMZN) Stock for the Next 10 Years: Buy, Hold, or Avoid?

Should you stay invested in the e-commerce and cloud leader?

Amazon (AMZN +2.20%), the world's largest e-commerce and cloud infrastructure company, has delivered an impressive 534% gain over the past ten years. But does its stock still have more upside potential over the next decade?

Amazon generates most of its revenue from its e-commerce business, but its cloud platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS), brings in most of its operating profits.

AWS already hosts tens of millions of websites and apps, and it's helping its developers build and train new generative AI apps on platforms like Bedrock and SageMaker. Amazon has also been producing its own first-party AI accelerators, and it owns nearly a fifth of Anthropic -- the rapidly growing AI company that plans to go public by the end of 2026.

All of those AI catalysts for AWS -- along with the expansion of its e-commerce business into higher-growth overseas markets and the growth of its higher-margin advertising business -- could drive its earnings growth over the next decade.

Amazon's growth rates are impressive, but its expansion will be costly. It expects its capex to reach $220 billion in 2026 (up from $131.8 billion in 2025) and to rise further in 2027. That increased spending -- and competition from other hyperscalers -- could compress AWS' margins. That pressure could also make it tougher for Amazon to expand its lower-margin retail business.

Rising interest rates will make it more expensive for Amazon to expand its AI infrastructure, reduce the market's demand for its cloud services, and compress its valuation. Inflation, which has been exacerbated by the Iran war and the Trump Administration's unpredictable tariffs, could also throttle the growth of its retail business (including Whole Foods).

I initially invested in Amazon in early 2016, and I only sold a quarter of my position after the stock quadrupled from my average purchase price. I've been holding the rest since then, and I don't plan to sell my shares because it's still one of the easiest ways to stay invested in the booming e-commerce, cloud, AI, and digital advertising markets.

If Amazon matches analysts' estimates through 2028, grows its EPS at a 15% CAGR through 2036, and trades at 25 times its current year's earnings, its stock would more than quadruple to nearly $1,120 over the next decade. That ride could be bumpy, but I plan to stick with Amazon -- even though it's already my top position and accounts for nearly 10% of my portfolio -- for the foreseeable future.

#3166. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Fun Fact →  While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3165. Firefox’s new Mini Window is every multitasker’s dream – Chrome can’t do this

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The open-source browser's newest feature lets you pop out a page - or part of a page - into its own mini window. See why this is incredibly cool.

The developers at Mozilla are always hard at work to make Firefox the most useful browser on the market. To that end, they’ve added a new feature (still in beta), called Mini Window. I started using Mini Window as soon as it appeared in Firefox Nightly, and I’ve been very happy with how it performs.

Also: Why I’m sticking with Firefox as my browser

The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window. Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app. Essentially, I can move a page (or section) into what looks like a browser window, minus the browser bits. At first blush, there’s no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it.

However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/foward/reload buttons, and the window close button– and that’s it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.

Also: Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined

On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I’m working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy.

Using the Firefox Mini Window feature is quite simple, but until the feature comes out of beta, it can only be found in Firefox Nightly. I’ve been using Nightly as my default browser on both Linux and MacOS for some time now and have yet to run into a problem (YMMV).

For those who don’t want to risk using a potentially less-than-stable alpha version of Firefox, know that the Mini Window feature is slated to move to stable on November 10. Update Firefox on that day and can start enjoying the feature without upgrading to Nightly.

Until then, you can test Mini Window by installing Firefox Nightly, which can run alongside the stable Firefox release.

Also: Firefox just fixed my biggest annoyance with web browsers

Once I installed Nightly, there was nothing more to do. I didn’t have to enable Mini Window, as it’s already there. I simply had to right-click on an open tab and select Move Tab > Move to Mini Window.

Once I did that, the mini window popped out and hovered over Firefox. If I hovered my cursor over the mini window, the address bar and title bar for the window appeared, so I could drag the pop-up to wherever I needed.

I could also open a specific section of a tab in a Mini Window. To do that, I highlighted the section in question, right-clicked the section, and then clicked Move Section to Mini Window.

Let’s say I’m writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them — even when working on a smaller display.

Here’s another use case I’ve found: When using MacOS’s Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window.

Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

The closest thing Chrome has to Mini Window is Picture-in-Picture mode and the Mini Player. The caveat to Chrome’s feature is that those two options are only used for video and media playback. The next closest thing Chrome has is the ability to save a website as a web app, which you could then open alongside the main Chrome window. That feature, however, isn’t nearly as flexible as Firefox’s Mini Window option, and it’s not guaranteed to always hover over the main window.

#3164. Don’t want a touchscreen? All premium MacBook Pros could have one soon, reports say

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New reports indicate the touchscreens are to become the standard on premium MacBook Pros.

According to reports, Apple will eliminate non-touch versions of the premium MacBook Pros as soon as next year. This would make touchscreen technology a defining feature of MacBook Pro laptops with the Pro and Max chipsets, separating them from the entry-level MacBook Pros with base-model chips.

The higher-end 16-inch MacBook Pro configurations without the touchscreen will be discontinued, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in the Power On newsletter, with the first models arriving in 2027.

Also: Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pros may be late, but they have one big advantage

The 14-inch MacBook Pro will remain the affordable option within the lineup and is unlikely to receive a touchscreen upgrade. It is predicted to feature an M7 processor and a redesigned thinner chassis.

The move widens the divide between entry-level Apple laptops and flagship models, and the price tag for the premium laptops is likely to reflect it. In 2027, buyers will face the decision about whether touchscreen technology justifies spending considerably more on the MacBook Pro.

Also: Forget the touchscreen MacBook – Apple’s new M6 is the laptop I recommend for most people

The MacBook Neo and MacBook Air remain Apple’s most affordable and midrange laptops, respectively. The 14-inch MacBook Pro will follow with a more premium price tag at $1,999, with the touchscreen model starting at $2,899. The introduction of the Neo this year opened up the MacBook to a market it previously had little sway in.

This leaves a large gap between the price differences of Apple’s lowest- and highest-end laptop offerings, further distinguishing mainstream consumers from Apple’s highest-end “pro” users.

However, the 14-inch MacBook Pro still serves Apple’s largest mainstream audience. It’s designed to give professionals who need more capabilities than a midrange laptop offers the option to buy premium features at a lower price than touchscreen models.

Also: How to use your TV as a computer monitor – before you buy a new one

In recent years, the biggest factors that have bumped a MacBook model up to a new price category have been processor performance, memory, graphics capabilities, and, to a lesser extent, display quality. Now, the touchscreen appears to be a major component.

The difference between a touchscreen MacBook Pro and a non-touchscreen model could fundamentally change how buyers evaluate and compare the MacBook Pro with other Apple laptops. Instead of simply deciding how much processing power consumers need, they might also have to decide whether a touchscreen is worth the steep price.

#3163. Investors Shoot for the Moon

The quantum computing space needs to make progress on error correction before quantum computers are useful.

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool contributors Jon Quast, Matt Frankel, and Tyler Crowe discuss:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Oct. 19, 2026.

Jon Quast: Investors are shooting for the moon. Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing starts now. Welcome to Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing. I'm your host today, Jon Quast, and I'm joined by Foolish contributors Tyler Crowe and Matt Frankel. We've got several things on the docket today, including some moonshots and a question from our mailbag.

But first up, we want to talk about quantum computing. On the Hidden Gems team, we are tracking several investing trends that are going to be very important for the future, including this one of quantum computing. We are considering the top companies. We're developing scoring systems around them, even portfolios. The first bit of news that we have comes from Alphabet, releasing a press release this past week, and then we also have something from Quantinuum, and we're going to break this down into two.

Tyler, I want to start with you. I'm going to throw you some questions here on Quantinuum, and what it is saying is a record-breaking error correction. But a couple of questions here for our listeners. Basically, can you talk about the differences between logical and physical qubits? Then why does quantum computing even need error correction in the first place?

Tyler Crowe: Well, first off, Jon, thanks for really tossing me some softballs here to start with the show. Let's start with quantum computing, because it's not exactly the simplest topic, and I am going to grossly oversimplify this. I know there's going to be a lot of people who know a lot more about the subject. Some technical experts probably listening to it are going to shout at me. But I'm going to try to get through this so most everyone can understand. Qubits are basically like the bits and bytes that we know on our classical computers. It's the way that we store the information. Physical ones are the method in which we store in physical space. All forms of quantum computing do it, and we have various ways of actually doing quantum computing, but all the methods basically manipulate known quantum properties like superposition and entanglement. I'm very glad that we do this on video now because I get to show you the deep research that I've been doing this for years. It's the book I've been reading my children: Quantum Entanglement for Babies. I'm sure that a lot of people are really going to know a lot more after they read up on that. But moving from physical to logical, to your question, physical qubits, again, manipulating the quantum properties of known atoms, things like that.

The logical is translating these manipulations. Using the information across many physical qubits, sometimes hundreds, thousands, sometimes even millions, to detect when any single physical qubit contains errors. It's a way of self-correcting for a very, very complex and honestly a delicate system. These systems have to be held at extremely low temperatures or in strong electromagnetic fields or anything like that. Any single physical qubit can sometimes act up. The idea being that we use logical qubits to make sure to self-correct for anything that any single physical qubit is doing wrong. Now, this brings us to the Quantinuum story, where what they have announced is that they have the lowest error rate, or in the business, it's called logical fidelity. Basically, it's saying that they are detecting about five errors over 1 million operations, and that's about 10 times better than the record that Quantinuum had set only a month ago. I think the big news and why actually the stock is moving quite a bit today because of it is because this is a major leap forward, and it's happening over a relatively short amount of time.

Jon Quast: Tyler, I'm all for you reading to your kids about quantum computing. I just hope that Schrödinger’s cat isn't in the book. That might damage some littles.

Tyler Crowe: No, Schrödinger's Cat, although a couple other ones that might be a little challenging for a 3-year-old.

Jon Quast: Matt, let's turn to you and talk about some Google news here. In the press release it had last week, it said it's working on something called magic state cultivation, reducing errors by 40X. It sounds weird to talk about magic states when we're talking about an investing podcast. Let me just say this. Magic states, basically, you need them to do powerful operations in quantum computing. They're single-use. Once you use up one of these things, they are gone. That's the problem because you need millions of them, and up to this point, we're using a method called distillation, basically taking a bunch of fuzzy magic states and distilling them into one clear, usable state. Google developing a different strategy here, cultivation: growing these from scratch and pruning out bad ones and using the good ones, but potentially a more efficient way to make them. The problem is, since they are single-use, the quantum computer is actually using compute power to make them, and most of the power is going just to make these magic states, leaving little for the actual operation it's trying to perform. Doing it more efficiently sounds good, but what else do we need to know from this Google release?

Matt Frankel: Well, I mean, first of all, I will say to Tyler, he did a really good job explaining. I have a physics degree, and I'm not sure I could do that much better of a job explaining quantum computing to the average person. The quantum technology and terminology is going to take some getting used to, for sure. I love you use words like magic and fuzzy, and that lead in right there. But in plain English, building an error-corrected quantum computer is only one part of producing superior performance to traditional computers. To unlock the real potential, you need these things called magic states. Like you said, the problem is, these are single-use, and making clean ones is not an easy process. Google itself has estimated that as much of 95% of a quantum computer's capacity is going to end up simply making these.

The new process called cultivation is a working solution to this problem. Here's why it matters. If magic states are going to eat up most of your hardware's capacity, then making them cheaper and easier shrinks the number of qubits that are needed to produce useful work. We're looking for a quantum computer that outperforms what currently exists through the computers that the three of us are using right now. Jon Quast: I feel like I need to point out here that both companies are saying that this is more testing that it's doing. Jon Quast: Matt, what do you think about open source?

Matt Frankel: Yeah, I mean, I would agree with what Tyler said that Google, Microsoft, and Amazon, they're mostly landlords when it comes to the AI trade. They provide the compute power. The open-source models still run in their clouds. That's a net positive for those companies in particular. But, I mean, open source can be a headache, as Tyler said. I mean, Stanford's latest AI index, that the gap between the best open-source models and the best closed models is about a 3% effectiveness rate. It's really not a big difference these days. But enterprise customers are for now, still paying for closed models. It makes up roughly 90% of enterprise production in AI. Big companies are willing to pay for reliability, security, and support. Where open source is the real threat, and it's not to these three companies, is pricing power. That's where the bust risk is. It's not necessarily open source, but it's the tech companies that are like Google, Microsoft, Amazon, that are investing hundreds of billions of dollars, being able to get a reasonable payback on their AI spending. If the pricing models are disrupted, then that might not be the case anymore, and you might see a slowdown.

Jon Quast: To the question here, that is what the risk is as far as the price-to-earnings ratio. Let's say that you have a company that's valued at 100 million and it's generating 10 million in profits. If the pricing power goes away, the profits go down to say, 2 million. It was trading at 10 times profits. Now it's trading at 50 times because the earnings went way down. That is where the price-to-earnings ratio, if it looks reasonable now, that doesn't necessarily tell you what's happening in the future. It does matter how that pricing holds up. The open source is a risk out there that we're monitoring. That was good commentary from Tyler and Matt, don't put everything on that price-to-earnings ratio.
