#3162. What Are Open-Weight AI Models?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

You might use a chatbot without thinking about who controls the model behind it. Then an update changes how it answers, or you want help with something private you’d rather keep on your computer.

An open-weight model lets you download the pretrained AI and run it yourself. You’ll need software to use it and a computer that can handle it, but you get to keep a working copy. While chatbots get most of the attention, image and video generators can also have open-weight options.

Downloading an AI model doesn’t necessarily give you unrestricted permission or reveal everything that went into making it, though. Sure, you get more autonomy in how you use AI, but the word “open” still leaves a lot unsaid. Here’s what open-weight models are, what you can do with them and what to consider before trying one for yourself.

In a chatbot, the AI model is the software that generates the answers. During training, the model learns patterns by adjusting billions of numerical values called neural network weights. When you ask a question, the model uses your prompt and those learned patterns to predict what text should come next, building its answer one piece at a time.

Developers of closed models, including those behind ChatGPT and Claude, keep their weights private. An open-weight model makes its trained weights publicly available. That means you can download them and run your own copy using compatible software.

“Whenever you open-weight a model, all the weights are all over the place on the internet, like on Hugging Face and other servers,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at AI company Mistral, tells CNET. “So it’s virtually impossible to cut access to this model.”

With a free model and app, you can chat locally without a subscription or usage fees. More importantly, a fully local setup also keeps your prompts and files off an AI provider’s servers.

Don’t worry if you’re not tech-savvy, because you won’t have to write code or open a terminal to do it. Desktop apps like LM Studio, Ollama and Jan let you download and run open-weight models with a simple install, giving you a ChatGPT-like interface right on your Mac or PC. You still need a computer that can handle your chosen model. Once everything is installed, you can keep chatting offline.

If you know how, you can also adapt the model through further training, where permitted by its license. You don’t have to train an entirely new model from scratch.

People often use these terms interchangeably, but they don’t mean quite the same thing. An open-weight model can also be open-source, but publishing the weights alone doesn’t qualify under the Open Source Initiative’s definition.

Developers must share the code used to train and run it. They must also provide enough information about the training data for a skilled person to build a model that works much the same way. The terms must allow people to use, study, change and share it.

Under the OSI definition, developers don’t have to share the data they used to train a model. The Free Software Foundation says that should be part of the deal, with users free to use and change the data themselves.

Some open-weight licenses limit business use, meaning a model might be free to download but off-limits for an app you want to sell. That kind of restriction would disqualify it under the OSI definition. An open-source license can still require you to keep the same terms when you share a version you’ve changed.

Chinese models currently lead independent AI testing company Artificial Analysis’s intelligence rankings for open-weight models. You may already know about DeepSeek, but there is also Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 family, which offer downloadable weights.

Some US alternatives come from the companies behind familiar chatbots. OpenAI offers gpt-oss models separately from ChatGPT, while Google has Gemma models. Meta has Muse Glimmer and added Muse Spark Open alongside its Llama models, and Nvidia has Nemotron.

You don’t have to stick with the chatbot giants, either. A US-based startup, Reflection, released Beam, whose weights are now available to download. Another US startup, Thinking Machines Lab, offers its model Inkling.

Europe has a contender in France’s Mistral AI. Its downloadable models include Mistral Large 3 and the smaller Ministral 3 family. The newer Mistral Large 4, dubbed Le Chonk, is available now with downloadable weights.

Not every model mentioned here will run on a laptop. Some larger models need server hardware, while smaller versions can run on personal computers or even smaller devices, like phones.

An open-weight model can still hallucinate when it’s running offline on your laptop. It can also carry biases from its training. Developers may publish weights while keeping training data private, leaving outsiders unable to fully check what went into them.

Performance varies by model and task, so openness alone won’t tell you whether it will beat a closed alternative.

The freedom to change a model also means people can weaken or remove its safeguards.

“Guardrails are necessary to open-weighting a model,” Stock says. When I ask how to keep them safe if people can remove those protections after downloading a model, Stock says, “With a lot of work, you can partially overcome the guardrails,” comparing the effort involved to do so to fine-tuning a model yourself.

Once people have downloaded copies, the original developer has limited control over what happens next. A company can cut off someone misusing its online service, and releasing a safer replacement won’t update everyone’s download.

Yet those same downloads allow independent researchers to examine models more closely and identify faults. Researchers can test changes themselves, rather than depend on the developer to investigate a complaint.

Microsoft and other companies cited that benefit in an open letter defending open weights after reports of potential US restrictions on Chinese models. They argued that keeping these tools available helps security teams defend against attackers using AI.

“When you open-weight a model, you’re essentially enabling the entire ecosystem to progress together,” Stock tells CNET.

Open-weight models can draft emails, summarize documents, analyze local files and help with coding just like cloud models. However, when you run one locally, its speed and ability to handle long documents depend on both the model and your computer’s memory and processing power.

Larger models usually run more smoothly on computers with plenty of memory or a powerful GPU, like a Mac with 16GB or 36GB RAM, though smaller models may work on an 8GB Mac.

If you already own the necessary hardware, it’s worth considering installing an open-weight model. But if you have to buy a new computer to run them, weigh that cost against a $20-per-month subscription for a cloud model.

You can also use some open-weight models through their developers’ own websites that run them for you, like DeepSeek and Kimi. That’s less work than downloading and running the model yourself, but your prompts go to the provider.

If you want occasional help writing an email and don’t mind using an online service, a hosted chatbot may suit you just fine. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude all have free plans, so avoiding a subscription doesn’t automatically require running your own AI.

Open weights give you the option to take more control yourself, not to mention keeping sensitive documents on your device. An assistant that keeps working when you don’t have access to the internet sounds great. So does being able to keep a model you like even after its developer retires the online one.

“You don’t want to live in a world in which someone can cut off access to your model,” Stock says.

The future also looks promising with open-weight models being installed on smaller devices. Google’s Gemma models include smaller versions for phones and laptops. Mistral has a similar range of models, including specialized ones intended for particular uses and devices.

“We also have models specialized in audio, for instance,” Stock says, “and those can fit literally on the smartwatch.”

#3161. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

#3159. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3158. Fox Corporation: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Fox's streaming platforms are generating fresh revenue without eroding traditional cable income, a rare feat in the shift away from pay-TV.

On its earnings call held on Nov. 2, 2026, to review its fiscal year 2027 first quarter ended Sept. 30, Fox Corporation (FOXA -0.76%) announced top-line revenue growth of 22% to $4.6 billion alongside record quarterly EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. The network is expanding its direct-to-consumer digital services to capture audience shifts as traditional pay-television subscriptions decline. Three things management said on the call stand out.

Fox 1, the company's subscription streaming service, is attracting viewers who do not buy traditional cable packages. That gives the service high incremental value because new sign-ups bring in fresh revenue without cannibalizing existing pay-television affiliate fees.

Tubi, the company's ad-supported streaming platform, increased revenue 35% year over year as total viewing time expanded 23%. Management expects structural profitability to follow as ad revenues scale across its cord-cutting audience.

Political ad spending reached record levels across local television stations, Tubi, and national sports networks. Live broadcasts like the FIFA Men's World Cup provided high-demand programming that supported overall advertising pricing power.

Operational momentum is accelerating across broadcast and digital assets, backed by $4.5 billion in cash. Management is prioritizing sports rights discipline, streaming engagement, and affiliate pricing power.

Fox plans to resume share repurchases this quarter while navigating pay-television shifts through its direct-to-consumer platforms.

#3155. T-Mobile Is Crediting Some New York Customers for Plan Price Hikes. See If You’re Eligible

Customers on T-Mobile One accounts could get a $25 gift card, a free 5G phone or credit toward a more expensive 5G phone.

T-Mobile is settling with the State of New York over an Attorney General’s Office investigation into whether the carrier failed to honor price promises for T-Mobile One plans advertised as “Price Guarantee Plans” on its 4G network between January 2017 and April 2019.

Affected active T-Mobile customers who leave the carrier will be able to collect a credit worth the last month’s payment and a $25 gift card.

Those who stay on and are still using an older phone can get a free 5G phone (worth up to $250) or credit up to $150 toward a more expensive 5G phone for lines that are still using 3G or 4G. Rates for their recurring monthly plans will stay the same until 2029.

As part of the agreement, T-Mobile is also making a one-time payment to the Attorney General’s office in the amount of around $98,000.

According to a press release issued by New York Attorney General Letitia James, an investigation by the office found that T-Mobile raised rates on those plans in 2024 by approximately $5 per line, a change that affected approximately 252,957 plans at the time. It also pegs the relief to be worth around $38 million in value.

“T-Mobile misled hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers by promising that it would never raise prices on their cellphone plans, only to do exactly that just a few years later,” said James in the release. “Consumers shouldn’t have to pay the price for a misleading sale.”

The office’s filed agreement notes that T-Mobile made the price guarantee in at least two press releases and during a CNET video interview with then-CEO John Legere, pictured above, in 2017. In that video, Legere said, “We also extended the Un-contract to T-Mobile One Unlimited, which means we will never raise your rate; we guarantee.”

The agreement notes that T-Mobile ran afoul of a New York State law that requires companies to disclose terms “clearly and conspicuously,” and that any disclaimers about the price guarantee were ineffective by “directly contradict[ing] what a reasonable consumer would understand the Price Guarantee Offer to mean.”

It also states that “Respondent [T-Mobile] neither admits nor denies the OAG’s Findings” that detail the investigation’s conclusions.

When asked about the agreement, T-Mobile sent the following statement to CNET: “The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments. The agreement provides for approximately $98,000 paid to the state and a range of optional customer benefits. We’re glad to have this matter resolved and remain focused on delivering value to our customers.”

Per the agreement, T-Mobile has 150 days starting Oct. 20 to identify and notify customers who are eligible for the relief. After they’ve been notified, customers will have 45 days to decide whether to cancel their T-Mobile account (getting the last month’s payment and a $25 cash card) or continue as a customer (getting a free or discounted 5G-capable phone for each affected line or the $150 credit toward a new phone). For the latter, T-Mobile will also not charge any costs such as transfer or activation fees.

In 2024, The New York Times published a damning investigation into the program, revealing that, in some cases, data on drivers’ habits could be used by insurance companies to set rates. Some drivers saw significant premium increases after GM sold their driving history, and one owner was told a 22% premium increase resulted from driving information supplied by a data broker, according to a statement from the New York attorney general’s office.

The data collection was described as “spying,” and GM quickly ended the program that year. In 2025, GM settled with the Federal Trade Commission over Smart Driver and OnStar location data, agreeing to a five-year ban on selling driver data.

Attorneys general in many of the states involved in the $220 million settlement posted announcements about it, including Anthony G. Brown of Maryland.

The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or disclosing consumer driving and location data.

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson said.

Automobiles have evolved into computers on wheels over the last few decades, collecting vast amounts of data on drivers, including contacts and song lists, location data and diagnostic information. For GM, the issue was less about collecting data than about breaking its promise to customers that it wouldn’t sell it.

There may be more action to come on illegal or unethical data-collection practices in the auto industry.

“GM was the biggest case and, in some ways, presented the most egregious set of facts. But collecting and selling driving data is an industry norm, not an aberration,” said Peter Cassat, technology partner at CM Law and a former general counsel for Cox Automotive and New Country Motor Group.

“The difference now is that regulators have a template, and every state attorney general has seen a $220 million settlement, so I think we can expect more enforcement actions and settlements,” Cassat said.

“Vehicle providers should ask for driver consent feature by feature in plain English,” he said, not simply prompt buyers to check a box.

Beyond the touchscreen on your dashboard, modern vehicles run background systems that transmit data straight to the manufacturer, and drivers have little to no control over what gets collected or who buys it.

“Unfortunately, there isn’t a lot consumers can do,” he said. “Opt out wherever possible and don’t agree to unnecessary data sharing. Review your own Customer Disclosure Report to see whether driving data appears. And if your car has a modem that can be disabled, consider disabling it.”

#3151. The Wild World of Third-Party AI Apps for Ring Security, and Whether You Need Them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ring cameras offer broad capabilities, but third-party AI tools give HOAs, landlords and others even more ways to use them.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Basically, this software leverages Ring’s object recognition ability to use it for a wider range of monitoring possibilities. I’m trying out some of these apps to see just how they work, but if you or people in your neighborhood use Ring devices, you should know what they’re capable of. These mini apps range from casual fun to Flock-like levels of surveillance. Most require a Ring subscription and an additional monthly fee, typically a few dollars. Here are popular examples of those apps, how they work, if they’re legal and what they could be doing in your neighborhood.

For those annoyed by illegal trash dumping or other waste violations, the DumpWatch app promises to watch for trash miscreants using Ring’s AI for about $8 per month. The app records footage whenever it detects large amounts of waste being left in the camera’s field of view and creates a timestamped PDF that can be used to submit a complaint or file a police report.

Note that some examples DumpWatch uses show trash bins left on the sidewalk, a common occurrence on collection days, or extra trash placed beside bins, which may be allowed by local waste companies. It’s not guaranteed to capture only illegal activity.

Yes, these little apps can also serve as tools for homeowners associations if your neighborhood has strict rules about what’s permitted. One example is the $3 per month LawnWatch app, which is trained to monitor properties for HOA violations such as leaving toys cluttering a lawn, dog owners not cleaning up poop and so on. A somewhat more benevolent app, Greenlapse, tracks grass and plant growth over time, and is primarily designed to monitor your own landscaping projects.

Ring’s app store includes a slew of monitoring apps made specifically to track tenants and short-term rental guests, collecting info for landlords to use. One example is the $5-per-month ZoneGauge app, which continuously tracks how many people are in a space, letting owners know when someone is throwing a party, for instance.

Another option is the GuardCat app. It’s $8 per month and it summarizes guest check-outs, cleaner visits, “house rule violations” and more based on what Ring security cameras pick up using AI detection.

A quick reminder here: Companies such as Airbnb have banned indoor security cameras entirely. Apps like these shouldn’t be used indoors at all.

Using AI to monitor pets for unusual behavior that could signal health problems is nothing new. We’ve reviewed quite a few pet cameras and smart tracking collars that do something similar. But apps such as Pet Vet AI can use Ring cams as an alternative for $10 per month. Here, the app analyzes pet snapshots for issues such as limping, throwing up food, sleeping in unusual spots and more, then summarizes any problems for pet owners. The app says it works with birds, reptiles and fish, too, but I’ve never seen pet AI advanced enough to get any worthwhile analysis from the non-mammals in our homes.

Ring’s mini apps extend beyond the home and into many aspects of the workplace, too. Apps such as ProofClock and TimeStack are designed for construction, freight and similar industries to monitor when teams arrive at a location and how long they work, even when the Ring camera owner isn’t present. Some of these apps can also generate uptime and service-level agreement reports, although I’m dubious about tying Ring AI, which isn’t always reliable, so closely to payroll.

We’ve tested plenty of bird feeder cameras that can identify bird species with varying degrees of success. But if you’d like to point a Ring camera at a feeder or birdbath, an app such as What’s That Bird.AI can do something similar for $5 per month. It captures screenshots of nearby birds and attempts to identify them so you can see which species are stopping by.

There’s a small problem here: Feeders from Birdbuddy and similar brands give you bird recognition for free, so if you don’t mind buying a dedicated bird watching camera, there’s no need to pay a subscription at all.

No. Each app has its own requirements, displayed on their download pages. Some will work with nearly any Ring device that uses a camera. Others require a wired-in Ring device or a more recent Ring camera from the past year or so, or both.

Keep in mind that tools like these aren’t perfect and shouldn’t be the sole basis for filing a complaint or taking other action. They’re also expensive for what they do — such as charging $5 per month just to tell you when your mail arrives — so I don’t think they’re worth the cost for the average user. One exception may be pet AI, which could replace more expensive pet camera services. Either way, it’s important to know your options — and which apps your neighbors may be using.

The iPhone Duo is a $1,999 phone that, in case it wasn’t obvious from the price, isn’t for everyone. #3149. Daylight Saving Time Ends Sunday. Get Ready to Change Your Clocks

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of the US gains an hour of sleep this weekend, but Hawaii and most of Arizona won’t change their clocks.

It’s time to change your clocks: Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, when clocks across most of the US move back to 1 a.m.

The timing lines up neatly with Halloween — trick-or-treaters on Saturday still get the later sunset, and the extra hour of sleep arrives overnight. Phones and computers update on their own, but oven, microwave and car clocks usually don’t.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March. Here’s what else to know about the switch, including which states skip it — and when the clocks spring forward again.

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates. The UK, for example, fell back last weekend.

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located.

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.

Read more: Why Is NASA Working on a Time Zone for the Moon?

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

#3148. November 2026 Skywatching Guide: Meteors, Planets, Stars and a Full Moon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

This month, you'll find three meteor showers and a planetary alignment starring four planets.

Autumn is marching right along, and so are the objects in the night sky. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time ending Nov. 1, the sun will set even earlier. That’ll give skygazers more time to see some cool sights without staying up horribly late or waking up unbearably early.

This month of fall is arguably the most active for amateur astronomers, with things to see as early as Nov. 2 and as late as Nov. 30. While there aren’t any major celestial events, a series of smaller ones makes up for it.

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, where it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

The month begins with a meetup among Mars, Jupiter and the moon. The three will appear close together in the night sky, making them easy to spot: The moon is easy to find, and both planets are visible to the naked eye. On Nov. 2, the moon will be closer to Mars, and the trio will follow one another across the sky throughout the night. Regulus will also be in tow and readily visible to the naked eye.

Nov. 3 continues the good vibes. The moon slides over to the other side of Regulus on that night, but all four celestial bodies are still quite close together and easy to spot. Mars, Jupiter and Regulus will get even closer to each other as November progresses, but the moon moves even further away after Nov. 3.

The Southern Taurids have technically been active since Sept. 20, and continue until Nov. 20. This long-running meteor shower peaks during the evening of Nov. 4 and morning of Nov. 5. It’s not a terribly strong meteor shower and should average about five meteors per hour. However, it often tosses bright fireballs, so what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality.

The moon is 22% illuminated that night, which the American Meteor Society calls “favorable conditions” for viewing a meteor shower. You want to get as far away from light pollution as possible to give yourself even better odds, and make sure to dress for the weather. The Southern Taurids will appear to originate from the Taurus constellation, which rises in the east shortly after sunset and moves across the sky before setting in the west right before sunrise.

It’s no secret that the full moon is usually the most popular celestial event to happen every month, but skygazers also value the new moon. This is because the moon is a significant source of light pollution, making many stars and planets, such as Uranus and Neptune, harder to see. With the new moon on Nov. 9, it’ll be the darkest night of November — and perfect for stargazing and night-sky photography.

Nov. 9 also happens to be Carl Sagan Day, an unofficial holiday to honor the visionary astronomer. If you’re stuck inside that night, you can always use the occasion to watch Sagan’s legendary Cosmos series, which is available for free on the Internet Archive or through various user uploads on YouTube.

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Nov. 14 there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Nov. 14 and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 11 and the morning of Nov. 12. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Nov. 11, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It starts on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41%-illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon.

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object so you can find it.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

#3147. You Can End Spammy Election Phone Calls Now With This iPhone Trick

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The election is almost over, and you can end spam calls now.

Election day is a few days away, and that means political campaigns are mounting one last push to advocate for their candidate and issue. So you might be getting more election-related phone calls than usual. While those calls are well-meaning, they can be annoying if you’ve already voted early or have made up your mind about who to vote for. Luckily, if you keep your iPhone updated to the most recent iOS version, you can enable call screening on your device.

Apple introduced call screening in iOS 26. It isn’t an Apple Intelligence feature, so any iOS 27-compatible iPhone, such as the iPhone 14 Pro, can use it. I enabled the feature over a year ago and my iPhone has diligently held back spam calls, like the Hoover Dam, ever since. But you have to enable it first.

Here’s how to enable call screening in a few easy steps and what to know about the new feature.

1. Tap Settings.2. Tap Apps near the bottom of the menu.3. Tap Phone.

Under the section Screen Unknown Callers, you’ll see three options: Never, Ask Reason for Calling and Silence. Here’s what you should know about each of these options and which one is right for most people.

Choosing Never is the default option and lets calls from unsaved numbers come through and ring on your phone. It also documents missed calls in your Recents list in your Phone app, just like before call screening was available.

If you tap Ask Reason for Calling, your iPhone will ask anyone who calls you from an unsaved number why they are calling you without ringing your iPhone. After the caller answers a few questions, your iPhone will notify you with a transcript of the caller’s answers. Then you can decide whether you want to answer the call.

You can also pick Silence, which is the nuclear option for phone calls. Any unsaved numbers that call you will be silenced and sent to voicemail, no questions asked.

Ask Reason for Calling is the best option for most people who want to screen calls. I chose it, and while it notified me when scam callers answered some questions, which they rarely did, it also notified me when my doctor’s office called to go over some test results. If I had chosen Silence, I would have missed my doctor’s office (and choosing Never would mean checking every call if I was expecting something important).

If you choose Ask Reason for Calling and dislike it, you can always follow the steps above again and choose one of the other options. And remember, you can always silence your iPhone and not be bothered by any phone calls at all. My wife has not taken her phone off silent in months, and she remains blissfully unbothered by spam calls.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.1 as well as our iOS 27 cheat sheet for other tips and tricks.

#3146. This Has Been the Best-Performing Stock in the "Magnificent Seven" This Year, and It's Not Even Close

Most of the leading tech stocks have underperformed the S&P 500 in 2026.

The "Magnificent Seven" stocks are a collection of the leading tech stocks in the world. But this year, they haven't been doing well. The S&P 500 has surprisingly been outperforming nearly all of them. It's particularly surprising given that the broad index is up only 11%. It's doing well, but that doesn't seem like a high bar for stocks to exceed.

Yet, there's only one stock in the Magnificent Seven that has been able to beat it. Ironically, it's the company that has been a bit of a laggard when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI): Apple (AAPL -1.83%). Year to date, it's up around 25%.

What's behind its rally, and could it go even higher?

While many tech companies are in an aggressive arms race in developing AI chatbots and models as quickly as possible to stay ahead of the competition, Apple's been far more modest by comparison. In fact, customers have become frustrated with its slow pace with respect to AI offerings and its iPhones lagging behind rival phones.

As other stocks in the Magnificent Seven have been spending hundreds of billions of dollars and ramping up spend, Apple modestly forecast $14 billion in capex for its entire fiscal year, unchanged from a year ago. It's perhaps no coincidence then, as investors have become more concerned about high levels of AI spend, that Apple's been the stock of choice among tech investors.

Having a more sensible, calculated, and less aggressive approach to capex has endeared it to the broader market.

Apple has a terrific business, but the problem is that its stock is now trading at an exceptionally high premium -- close to 40 times its trailing earnings. That's a particular concern for a business that in recent years hasn't often generated more than single-digit growth. There have been times when it's fared better, but also times when it's even performed worse.

Paying such a high premium for fast, high-growth business may be justifiable, but that's not representative of what Apple is. It's a safe, stable tech stock, but it's not what I'd consider to be fast-growing by any means.

Investors who buy the stock at such elevated levels should tread carefully, as it could be vulnerable to a correction in the near future, especially if its upcoming results prove to be underwhelming. Apple is a quality stock to hold for the long haul, but I wouldn't buy it at its current price, as its future returns may be minimal, and at worst, the stock could experience a significant decline given its inflated value.

#3145. 200,000 Folds and Counting for the iPhone Duo. How Far Can Our Fold-a-Phone Take It?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

We're folding Apple's iPhone Duo over and over -- 900 times an hour -- to test the durability of its hinge.

Happy November! The air is getting chillier, retailers are shifting from Halloween to the holidays, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to test Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than a week ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? On Monday, Nov. 2, we passed 200,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#3143. Robinhood Markets vs. Interactive Brokers: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Interactive Brokers is a highly profitable global broker with a debt-free balance sheet. Robinhood is a fast-expanding challenger whose results still swing with trading activity.

The shift toward digital trading has created a fierce rivalry between established players and agile newcomers. Deciding between Robinhood Markets (HOOD -1.35%) and Interactive Brokers Group (IBKR -2.69%) requires balancing rapid growth against global stability.

Robinhood focuses on accessible, user-friendly mobile trading for retail audiences, whereas Interactive Brokers targets professional traders with sophisticated tools and access to global markets. As both companies expand their offerings into new asset classes, investors must determine which business model is best positioned to capture market share in the evolving financial landscape.

Robinhood Markets operates as a multifaceted financial services platform offering retail brokerage, cryptocurrency trading, and digital banking services. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended December 2025, the company highlighted a customer base of nearly 28.7 million funded accounts. The acquisition of Bitstamp in 2025 allowed the firm to begin serving institutional customers with services like on-exchange lending and perpetual futures for Bitcoin (BTC -1.25%).

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $4.5 billion, representing a significant increase of approximately 51.6% over the previous year. The company reported a net income of roughly $1.9 billion for the period, resulting in a net margin of about 42.1%. This performance indicates a substantial turnaround from the net loss reported in FY 2023, showing much stronger bottom-line results for the business.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 1.3x. This ratio, which measures total debt against shareholder equity, suggests the company uses a moderate amount of leverage to fund its fintech stocks operations. Robinhood also reported a current ratio of roughly 1.3x, which measures its ability to cover short-term obligations, and generated nearly $1.6 billion in free cash flow. Free cash flow represents the cash remaining after subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash.

Interactive Brokers Group provides direct-access trade execution and clearing services across approximately 175 market centers globally. The company serves a diverse client base including individual investors, hedge funds, and registered investment advisors. Its primary value proposition lies in low-cost execution and a platform capable of handling multiple currencies and asset classes simultaneously.

For FY 2025, the company reported revenue of close to $10.2 billion, which was a growth of nearly 9.8% compared to the prior year. Net income for the period was approximately $984 million, reflecting a net margin of roughly 9.6%. Interactive Brokers has shown a consistent trend of increasing net income over the last three fiscal years as it scales its global footprint and account numbers.

According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.0x. This indicates that Interactive Brokers carries very little debt relative to its shareholder equity. The firm also reported a current ratio of approximately 1.1x and generated an impressive $15.7 billion in free cash flow, defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, providing significant liquidity for its global operations.

Robinhood Markets faces significant regulatory and legislative scrutiny regarding its payment for order flow and cryptocurrency practices. The company also deals with risks from rapid operational expansion and its heavy reliance on third-party liquidity providers. Furthermore, significant litigation exposure and market systemic risks could impact trading volumes on its platform, specifically regarding the Robinhood 24 Hour Market.

Interactive Brokers Group operates in a highly competitive industry where research-driven firms like Morningstar (MORN +5.54%) and other electronic brokerages put constant pressure on commission-based revenue. The firm is exposed to clearing and execution risks, including potential credit losses from customer margin loans and counterparty defaults. Additionally, the company relies heavily on proprietary technology, making it vulnerable to system failures or cybersecurity threats that could disrupt its global trading services.

Interactive Brokers Group offers a lower Forward P/E, which measures market price against future earnings estimates, while Robinhood Markets carries a higher P/S ratio. The P/S ratio evaluates market capitalization relative to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with Interactive Brokers. What tipped it for me is that it is adding customer accounts faster than Robinhood while keeping far more of its revenue as profit, a good balance of growth and stability. In Q3 2026, Interactive Brokers posted record pretax income at a 78% margin, and customer accounts grew 35% from a year earlier. It also raised its dividend and is testing AI agents that can trade on a customer's behalf.

To give Robinhood its due, its offerings continue to grow. Q3 2026 revenue hit a record as prediction markets and banking caught on with customers. But crypto revenue fell by more than half and earnings per share declined, which weighed on the stock.

For investors thinking in years rather than quarters, a broker that continues to add customers while remaining profitable has room to reward shareholders for a long time. With no debt to repay, Interactive Brokers is built to keep doing that even when markets turn rough.

#3142. On the Eve of the Midterms, AI Data Centers Have Become a Bipartisan Headache

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With the midterms tomorrow, surveys from ABC News, NBC News and CNBC all show that majorities oppose new AI data centers near their communities.

A single large AI data center can use as much electricity as tens of thousands of homes, and residents in a growing number of communities worry about what that could mean for their utility bills. That concern has carried over from public hearings into tomorrow’s midterm elections.

Recent polls show majorities of Democrats and independents, along with a sizable share of Republicans, oppose new data centers in their areas. That leaves candidates in both parties answering questions about projects once courted by state and local leaders. Supporters say the facilities bring jobs, tax revenue and an advantage in AI development.

Further, a new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community.

Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.

Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.

Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue.

As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.

The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026.

A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room.

According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide.

“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.

Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.

The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.
