#3139. Stop Charging Your Phone to 100%. Here’s What to Do Instead

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A few changes to when and how you charge, plus one built-in setting, can keep your phone’s battery healthier for longer.

A phone running a game while plugged into a fast charger gets hot, and that heat wears down the battery faster than almost any other charging habit. Leaving it at 100% for hours causes similar damage more gradually. Both habits are easy to avoid once you know what to watch for, and most phones now include settings that can help. Here’s what to change in your routine.

Voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss. The damage may not appear immediately, but it’s measurable after one year and obvious after two.

Age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably. Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity faster when they spend extended time at the top of their charge range, which is precisely where an overnight charge leaves them. The fix doesn’t require a new phone or even a new charger. It requires a small adjustment to a habit most people have never thought twice about.

Keeping a lithium-ion cell pinned at 100% creates voltage stress, and the heat generated from sitting on a charger could end up meaning the difference between keeping your current phone a little longer or having to buy a new one. So once and for all, does keeping your phone plugged in really hurt the battery? Here’s what the experts suggest.

It isn’t about immediate damage but rather how fast your battery ages over time. Understanding the difference between what will and won’t break your phone is key. Here is the truth about your charging habits.

Battery health is not just about how many times you charge your phone. It is also about how it manages voltage, temperature and maintenance. Lithium-ion batteries age fastest when they are exposed to extreme levels: 0% and 100%.

Keeping these batteries near full charge for long stretches of time puts additional voltage stress on the cathode and electrolyte. This is why many devices use “trickle charging” or temporarily pause at 100%, topping up only when needed.

Still, the biggest threat is not overcharging, but heat. When your phone is plugged in and running demanding apps, it produces heat that accelerates chemical wear inside the battery. If you are gaming, streaming or charging on a hot day, that extra warmth does far more harm than leaving the cable plugged in overnight.

The Apple battery guide describes lithium-ion batteries as “consumable components” that naturally lose capacity over time. To slow that decline, iPhones use Optimized Battery Charging, which learns your daily routine and pauses charging at about 80% until just before you typically unplug, reducing time spent at high voltage.

Apple also advises keeping devices between 0 and 35 degrees Celsius (32 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit) and removing certain cases while charging to improve heat dissipation. You can read more on the official Apple battery support page.

Samsung offers a similar feature called Battery Protect, found in the One UI battery and device care settings. When enabled, it caps charging at 85%, which helps reduce stress during long charging sessions.

Other Android makers like Google, OnePlus and Xiaomi include comparable options — often called Adaptive Charging, Optimized Charging or Battery Care — that dynamically slow power delivery or limit charge based on your habits. These systems make it safe to leave your phone plugged in for extended periods without fear of overcharging.

Even with these safeguards, some conditions can accelerate battery wear. As mentioned before, the most common culprit is high temperatures. Even for a short period of time, leaving your phone charging in direct sunlight, in a car or under a pillow can push temperatures into unsafe zones.

Heavy use, such as gaming or 4K video editing, while charging can also cause temperature spikes which can degrade the battery faster. And cheap, uncertified cables or adapters may deliver unstable current that stresses cells. If your battery is already several years old, it will naturally be more sensitive to this kind of strain.

There is no need to overhaul your habits, but a few tweaks can help your battery age gracefully. Start by turning on the optimization tools on your phone: Optimized Battery Charging on iPhones, Battery Protect on Samsung devices and Adaptive Charging on Google Pixels. These systems learn your routine and adjust charging speed so your phone is not sitting at 100% all night.

Keep your phone cool while charging. According to Apple, phone batteries perform best between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit (16 to 22 degrees Celsius). If your phone feels hot, remove its case or move it to a better ventilated or shaded spot. Avoid tossing your phone under a pillow or too close to other electronics, like your laptop. Skip wireless chargers that trap heat overnight. Use quality chargers and cables from your phone manufacturer or trusted brands. Those cheap “fast-charge” kits you find online often deliver inconsistent current, which can cause long-term issues.

Finally, try not to obsess over topping off the charge. It is perfectly fine to plug in your phone during the day for short bursts. Lithium-ion batteries actually prefer frequent, shallow charges rather than deep full cycles. There is no need to keep it between 20% and 80% all the time, but just avoid extremes when possible.

Keeping your phone plugged in overnight or on your desk all day will not destroy its battery. That is a leftover myth from a different era of tech. Modern phones are smart enough to protect themselves, and features such as Optimized Battery Charging or Battery Protect do most of the heavy lifting for you.

Still, no battery lasts forever. The best way to slow the inevitable is to manage heat, use quality chargers and let the software on your phone do its job. Think of it less as “babying” your battery and more as charging with intention. A few mindful habits today can keep your phone running strong for years to come.

#3138. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3137. Why the Companies Most at Risk of Disruption Are Usually the Most Successful

Disruption rarely arrives from the direction an industry expects, and oftentimes, outside of the industry entirely.

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool contributor Rachel Warren talks with Jeffrey Cole -- founder of the World Internet Project, director of USC's Center for the Digital Future, and author of Disruptors at the Gate -- about:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Oct. 18, 2026.

Jeffrey Cole: The disruption of the retail business should have come from Walmart or Target, not an upstart bookseller in Seattle. The disruption of the taxi business, my God, was anything more right for disruption in taxis and just should have come from Yellow Cab or Hertz or Avis, not a bunch of computer nerds in the Silicon Valley who knew nothing about transportation, but knew a lot about algorithms to make things happen.

Rachel Warren: That was Jeffrey Cole, one of the world's leading voices on media, technology and the digital future and author of the new book Disruptors at the Gate. I'm Motley Fool analyst Rachel Warren. Jeffrey founded the World Internet Project, the longest-running global study of online behavior, and has spent more than three decades advising presidential administrations, the FCC, and the Department of Defense on exactly the kinds of changes that blind side companies and investors alike. In this conversation, we get into why disruption almost never comes from where an industry is watching what the history of AI, the Internet, and Kodak all have in common, and why the executives best positioned to fight disruption are almost structurally prevented from doing so. We hope you enjoy.

Welcome back to Motley Fool Conversations. I'm Motley Fool analyst Rachel Warren. Today, I'm delighted to be joined by Jeffrey Cole. Jeffrey is one of the world's leading voices on media, technology, and the digital future and has spent more than three decades tracking change and anticipating what comes next. He founded the World Internet Project. That’s the longest-running global study of online behavior spanning 27 years in 35 countries, and now directs the Center for the Digital Future at the USC Annenberg School. Jeffrey has advised four U.S. presidential administrations, the FCC, Congress, and the Department of Defense, along with global government leaders. His industry clients include Microsoft, Sony, Time Warner, AT&T, CBS. He also co-founded the Global Disruption Investment Fund and is the co-author of the upcoming book Disruptors at the Gate: When Visionaries, Trailblazers and Two Guys in a Garage Turned the World Upside Down. Jeffrey, so excited to have you on the show.

Jeffrey Cole: Rachel, I'm really thrilled to be here and thank you for such a nice introduction.

Rachel Warren: Of course. Maybe to set the stage for our audience, for your book and its core themes. Tell us about what led you to write this book, but also what are the major sectors and companies that you think are most deeply exposed to structural disruption in the coming years?

Jeffrey Cole: Well, as far as why I wrote it, I had been a television guy, and the most powerful medium ever invented when it began in the ‘40s. I watched as the Internet came along. I got a hunch. This is where the World Internet project came from. But the Internet was going to be pretty darned important. Turned out to be a lot more important than I or anyone could have predicted. But I watched how people responded. The Internet was a threat to a lot of businesses. In the book, I list about 100 companies or industries that have disappeared because of the Internet, starting with the yellow pages encyclopedias and going on, and yet no one really understood the nature of the threat. They doubled down on their behavior. They refused to acknowledge that something was changing because disruption, unlike innovation, which is just a change, which may lead to increased market share, disruption is something that comes from unexpected places, turns business models upside down, changes everything.

Historically, what I call master disruptions, disruptions that lead to dozens or hundreds of other changes, the Internet being one of those, but also the Industrial Revolution or the introduction of the automobile, that kind of disruption tends to occur about every 100-150 years. We're living through the third massive master disruption in 25 years. Started with the Internet. COVID, the unique thing about COVID, it was the first time that everyone everywhere at the same moment was disrupted. The way we did everything went online. I wrote a little piece during COVID, asking, what would the pandemic have been like if there were no Internet? The answer was a lot worse. Then AI is now the third in 25 years. We can already see the next one quantum computing, coming up the driveway. That I got interested in this massive change and why government leaders, and we're seeing that right now with a discussion over AI, why government leaders, why business leaders, and why people rarely are able to adapt very easily. The biggest disaster and disruption is denial.

Rachel Warren: One of the interesting things to think about right now in the age of the AI Revolution, which obviously there were many precursors to that, and it's been coming for a long time, but it seems as though everything has sped up all at once. I think there's been a lot of debate as to whether what we're seeing now in terms of its disruptive potential. Is this like nothing we've seen before? This is the first time something like this is happening or can we trace it through line to other disruptions?

Jeffrey Cole: We have seen disruptions that change, I mentioned, the Internet changed everything. But AI does take it to a new level. Look, the discussion we're having right now, literally as we speak, is AI going to end humanity by the end of the decade? I don't see that quite yet or hopefully ever. But the stakes have risen. Even if that turns out to be hype or fear mongering or there's nothing to it, the level at which AI is going to change. We know employment's one of the few areas I don't see a hopeful, easy outcome, but the way it's going to change access to information, it is unprecedented. We always want to think we're living in the middle of the biggest thing that's ever happened. But I thought the moment AI appeared, incidentally, AI, the joke within scientific laboratories and universities for 60 years was AI has a great potential, and it always will. Well, that changed when Chat was introduced at the end of 2022.

But AI, the moment it was introduced, I thought was as important a disruption as the beginning of the printing press. I now really do believe it's the most important disruption of all time. That's not hype, whether it can be the best thing that ever happened or the worst, or it looks like both, but certainly, an interesting distinction with the Internet. The Internet started with so much hope and optimism that it would connect people that anyone could be a journalist. Then we learned the dark underside of hate speech, bullying, misinformation. AI started with nothing but fear. Within three months of Chat being introduced, the OpenAI guys who created Chat were on stage at South by Southwest, which is probably the biggest tech bros conference where Twitter came out of, and they were talking about the benefits of AI. This is three lines after it came out, and they were booed offstage. Now, at graduations this year, you have speakers who foolishly are telling graduates living through the worst job market for graduates in the last 70 years in fear that there are no jobs. They're telling them all seize the opportunity, learn AI, and it's booing and jeering. The stakes are big.

Rachel Warren: It seems as though disruption almost never comes from where an industry or a company is watching, and I wonder, is there a discipline for auditing a company's vulnerability or an industry's vulnerability to these disruptive changes rather than just scanning the horizon?

Jeffrey Cole: It's darn tough because as you said, innovation comes likely from your competitor. Figures out a better way to do what you do and may gain market share. Disruption comes from completely unexpected places. The disruption of the retail business should have come from Walmart or Target, not an upstart bookseller in Seattle, and the disruption of the taxi business, my God, was anything more for disruption in taxis and just should have come from Yellow Cab or Hertz or Avis, not a bunch of computer nerds in the Silicon Valley who knew nothing about transportation, but knew a lot about algorithms to make things happen.

The disruption of the automobile business should have come from Toyota or General Motors, not from a South African immigrant who didn't know much about transportation. It does come from all these unexpected places that we use it in the subtitle of the book, but everybody knows this as two guys in a rage. You can eavesdrop or spy, not literally spy, on your competitor and try to get a sense of what they're doing. But how do you eavesdrop on two guys in a garage you've never heard of? That is very difficult. But one of the things we try to do in the book is the book goes through all the examples and lessons, but the last chapter is a battle plan. What do you do when the disruptors are at the gate?

The first stage is expect to be disruptive. Live your life as if you're going to be disruptive. When Larry Page and Serge Brin created Google in a Garage in Mountain View in the late 90s, they knew they didn't invent search. They had already been out to Vista and Ask Jeeves, and, of course, Yahoo. They knew they just did it so differently and better that the first moment anyone used Google, they didn't want to use anything else. It was as if Google could read your mind. Sometimes they would tell you with your search, did you mean to say, and it could read your mind. They knew they didn't invent search. They from Day 1 ran that company as if they were going to be disrupted. They had mechanisms in place. It happened, but it took 23 years, and by the time it actually happened, they had gotten complacent, as well. The disruption was AI in everything they were afraid of. Now, of course, Google's surviving AI. It's surviving beautifully.

But there is one big difference that's happened to Google. You look at Search. Google was over 90% of search in every country on the Earth with a couple of exceptions like North Korea and Iran. They had over 90% market share. When AI shakes out between Anthropic and Claude and Chat and Grok from Elon Musk, Google's going to probably end up at about 35, 40% market share, a great percentage. They may even be higher than almost anybody, but it's not 90. They did expect, so expecting to be disruptive. Looking around, not being complacent, understanding the whole thing can change in a moment. Those guys in a garage, trillion dollar industries can be created or destroyed.

Crank up Céline Dion: You can catch a glimpse into what Google was like back in 1998.

Nintendo is gearing up to release its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Thursday, and Google is marking the occasion with an Easter egg that transports the search engine back to 1998 – the year the original game was released.

If you go to Google.com now and search for “Zelda,” the game’s legendary Master Sword appears in the bottom right corner of the screen. In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the sword is a means to travel back and forth in time. (Searching for “Master Sword” also manifests the legendary weapon.)

When you click the sword, it thrusts into a pedestal and an animation plays before revealing a pre-2000s search page. In this view, you see the classic blue links, the I’m Feeling Lucky button and instead of seeing “Google” in the top-left corner of the page, you see the retro-looking “Google!” with an exclamation point. (Google removed the exclamation point from its logo in 1999.) If you stay real quiet and listen closely, you might also be able to hear Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On in the background.

What you won’t see on this page are any ads, AI overviews or random social media posts. It’s such a retro experience, and a fun reminder of what using Google was like back in the day. The neater, less cluttered layout made me feel instantly calmer than Google’s normal view.

However, this change isn’t permanent. As soon as you search for something else in this view, you’re transported back to the current version of Google Search. I wish there were an option to permanently enable this view, but for now, I’ll enjoy this slice of internet nostalgia.

#3133. The Swift Observatory Is Dropping Back to Earth This Week. Here’s What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of the space telescope is slated to burn up in the atmosphere, but some fragments may make their way down to Earth.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory — formerly known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — is in its final days. The space telescope was launched into orbit on Nov. 20, 2004. Almost 22 years to the day, it’s expected to come crashing back down on Wednesday.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA, said in a statement last month.

NASA says the telescope should hit the atmosphere on Nov. 4 at around 3:30 a.m. ET, but the agency acknowledges an 11-hour window during which reentry is possible. That means it could come down in the middle of the night or the middle of the day. Most of the telescope is likely to burn up in orbit, with only a few components expected to reach Earth.

The location where those components splash down depends entirely on when Swift reenters the atmosphere. However, NASA says that the surviving fragments are “limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude.” On a map, that would create a band around the middle of the Earth terminating just above and just below the equator.

“The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely — approximately 1 in 2,100,” NASA said in a statement. “NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.”

In preparation for Swift’s reentry, NASA shut down operations in late October after conducting its final observation on Oct. 20. It was orbiting at just 171 miles above Earth’s surface at that point, and the increased atmospheric drag prevented Swift from doing any further work. It was a bittersweet moment for those who worked on the project.

“It is a sad time at the Penn State Mission Operations Center, as we have carefully tended Swift to control its science operations, its health and safety, and responded to anomalies day or night, every day for 22 years,” John Nousek, director of mission operations for Swift and professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET.

Swift’s initial mission was a runaway success and helped advance science’s understanding of gamma-ray bursts and their role in phenomena such as the birth of black holes and the history of the early universe.

That initial mission ended on Nov. 4, 2004, but the observatory was doing so well that NASA left it up there to continue collecting data. Its name changed to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory on Jan. 10, 2018, in honor of pioneering NASA astrophysicist Neil Gehrels, who served as the agency’s chief of the Astroparticle Physics Laboratory from 1995 until his death in 2017.

The space telescope was designed to help solve the mystery of gamma-ray bursts by rapidly detecting them, determining their sources and then further analyzing them for study back on Earth. It also enabled unique sampling to observe newly discovered objects only minutes after their light reached Earth, said Nousek.

The amount of science conducted using Swift’s data cannot be overstated. According to NASA, it scanned over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, took 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope and sent home 12 TB of data. That data is showcased in an estimated 7,000 research papers, which averages out to just under one study per day over its 22-year run.

“We hope Swift has set the standard for time domain astrophysics,” Nousek said. The space telescope also helped pioneer many policies that ultimately shaped those discoveries, such as making data immediately accessible and providing over 1,000 guest investigators with the opportunity to use Swift throughout its long life, according to Nousek.

It’s only a stroke of bad luck that kept the observatory from floating for even longer. NASA attempted a rescue of Swift over the summer of 2026. However, after a series of engineering difficulties and control issues, the attempt was abandoned, sealing Swift’s fate. NASA turned the instruments back on and kept recording data as long as possible.

Research shows that people are drained by meetings – and AI tools exacerbate it. A new initiative by Visit Iceland aims to remind you of what matters most.

Is there anything worse than a meeting that really should have been an email? Visit Iceland has a new, albeit quirky, way to combat increasing meeting fatigue.

Rather than turning to AI tools and notetakers to take your place or keep track of what’s important in meetings, a real, crafty person will show up to listen. The AI Knittakers initiative from Visit Iceland will let you book an authentic Icelandic knitter to join your virtual meeting who will knit a sign with a single word that sums up the meeting, like “align,” “pivot,” “reset,” “huh?” or, my personal favorite, “WTF?”

Meeting fatigue is real. A December 2023 survey of 5,000 workers found that 78% of respondents said work meetings make it hard for them to get their work done, and 76% said they feel drained on heavy meeting days, highlighting that the growing number of virtual meetings since the COVID-19 pandemic is both ineffective and exhausting. Many stressed-out workers (65%) are now turning to AI notetakers to sometimes attend meetings for them.

“An AI notetaker hears every word,” said Salka Sól Eyfeld, the program’s chief AI Knittaker. “A knitter hears the sigh. We listen for the one thing that actually matters, and then we knit it.”

The initiative is available now and will run through Nov. 20.

The booking couldn’t be simpler: Pick an available Knittaker from the website, book them during a meeting when your schedules align and give your coworkers the surprise of a lifetime while you do something more fun. The AI Knittaker will also email you a photo of your knitted one-word meeting summary, with the option to have it shipped to you if you live in Europe or the US.

According to the press release, some Knittakers will also be available to attend meetings in languages other than English. Just explore the list of Knittakers to see their language capabilities.

The idea of giving your coworkers a shock while also making a statement about your precious work time sounds appealing, but it also signals a broader global attitude.

People are drained by meetings, and AI tools exacerbate it. A recent study in Harvard Business Review found that certain uses of AI tools, such as switching between different chatbots, can lead to cognitive fatigue they call “brain fry.”

After conducting a survey that found that workers spend about 8 hours per month in meetings that they deem unnecessary, Visit Iceland wanted to remind you that there’s more to life than just work meetings. The solution is both deeply analog and deeply Icelandic.

Knitting is a big part of everyday life in Iceland, according to Visit Iceland, and is a common hobby for relaxation and socialization. Icelanders are often knitting lopapeysas, Iceland’s distinctive patterned jumpers made of lopi wool, in public and even during meetings. By joining the work call, the AI Knittakers will give you a glimpse of their culture and stunning surroundings, reminding you of how good life can be when it’s not dominated by work and technology.

“It’s easy to assume that every modern problem needs a technological answer,” said Sigríður Dögg Guðmundsdóttir, spokesperson for Visit Iceland. “In Iceland, we’ve found that some of the best answers are the simplest ones: a little more time, a little more nature and people who really listen to each other.

“With AI Knittakers, we’re sharing a little of that Icelandic perspective with the world, and we hope it inspires people to step away from their screens and perhaps come and experience Iceland for themselves,” she added.

#3131. Jean-Luc in Blue Jeans: Picard Cosplay Taught Me How Much Patrick Stewart Is Loved

My husband was assimilated at an Emerald City Comic Con, and even the Borg adored him. Thank you, Patrick Stewart.

Star Trek fans never doubted the amount of love the community had for Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday at age 86. But I experienced that love firsthand. Back in 2021, my husband, Rob, dressed as Captain Jean-Luc Picard for Emerald City Comic Con in Seattle, and the adoration he received, simply for cosplaying Stewart’s beloved character, was overwhelming.

Our planning wasn’t complicated. Looking for a costume that would go with his shaved head, and being a big fan of the show, it made sense for him to put on a red and black Star Trek uniform shirt, pin on a combadge and four pips to denote the Starfleet rank of captain, and step into some black shoes. Except for his glasses (and mask since this was 2021, the second year of the COVID-19 pandemic), it was an eerily accurate look.

Read more: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86

Once we walked into the Seattle Convention Center for the con, it was as if the real Patrick Stewart had shown up. The respect Stewart had built up for Picard transferred seamlessly to his lookalike. Just walking around with Rob made me feel like a celebrity escort. We couldn’t travel more than a few feet without someone noticing and calling out to him, always with glee, always with respect.

“Hey, Captain! Captain!”“Jean-Luc!”“Make it so, sir!”“Engage!”“Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!”

Rob didn’t even wear costume-authentic black pants. In a hurry to get out the door and not expecting this level of attention, he had just pulled on his jeans. That led to a few of the funnier comments.

“Hey Captain! Was it casual day on the bridge?”

Comic Con attendees go all out. There were eerily realistic characters from Star Wars, Pokemon creatures, groups of friends dressed as The Incredibles, at least five Spider-Men, the Doctor from Doctor Who and exquisite, elaborate characters from anime. Many, many people had put more time, money and sweat equity into their costumes than we did, but few received such a universally awed reception.

Read more: Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles

Other Star Trek characters were also portrayed, for sure. Two separate Will Rikers, Picard’s trusted “Number One,” raced up to us at different times to take photos with their captain. One woman cosplaying as Kathryn Janeway, captain of the USS Voyager from Star Trek: Voyager, also posed with Rob for a two-captain photo.

And then, they saw us. A group of Comic Con attendees dressed as the Borg, the villainous cyborgs who take Picard hostage to assimilate him and temporarily turn him into Locutus of Borg.

These Borg did not throw their costumes together last-minute. They could have walked off a Hollywood set. They had working lights on their outfits, ocular and cranial “implants,” corpse-like face makeup, arms built into cybernetic tools. Of the Borgs, three were towering men and one was a woman. The woman played the Borg Queen, her bald head covered in white makeup, elegant and terrifying.

The minute the Borg saw Rob’s Picard in the convention center crowd, they came after him. Resistance, as they say in the show, was futile.

Thankfully, they were a jollier sort than the television Borg, and after one joke about his casual-day jeans, they whisked him away to stroll around as a group and snap photos.

These Borg were so realistic that I felt a bit unnerved the entire time he was gone — and relieved when they returned him unharmed, thanked us, waved and headed on their way. I’m sure there were other serendipitous meetups between cosplayers at the convention, but this one was amazing to see and even more so to be even a small part of.

We’ve been to Emerald City Comic Con other times. Our daughter has cosplayed a variety of characters, and Rob once went as Dr. Stone, a science prodigy with green-tipped white hair (which required a wig). People in the know enjoyed that cosplay, too, and he was similarly asked to pose for photos.

But the sheer love we experienced when he dressed as Captain Picard was like nothing I’ve ever felt. Since his death, I’ve seen Stewart called a generation’s space dad, and there’s truth in that. People at the convention were delighted to see their space dad, even if just a doppelganger. It buoyed us along on an unexpected high on that cold December day in 2021.

In the famous Star Trek: Next Generation episode Darmok, Picard is trapped on a planet with the Tamarian captain, Dathon. They can’t understand each other. The entire Tamarian language is constructed out of mythological and historical metaphors, none of which Picard knows

Slowly, Picard begins to comprehend. He figures out that one of the most frequent phrases, “Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra!” references Darmok and Jalad, warriors who united on the island of Tanagra and eventually became friends, just like he and Dathon.

But there’s another phrase I’ve been thinking of lately. “Kiazi’s children, their faces wet.” An online Tamarian dictionary translates it as “downplaying the severity of a perceived injury.”

There’s no downplaying this loss. We’re all Kiazi’s children today. Our faces wet.

#3127. Palantir Grows Revenue 96% as New Deals Slow: Rapid Earnings Reaction

Palantir's latest quarter showed a business turning rapid growth into heavy profit. Here's what drove it and where the numbers look softer.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR -3.13%) grew third-quarter revenue 96% to about $2.31 billion and raised its full-year outlook again. Shares were up about 2% in after-hours trading. The business is turning growth into profit at a rare pace. But new contract signings barely grew, so future growth depends on signings picking up.

U.S. commercial revenue passed U.S. government revenue for the first time, with government at $953 million. Government contracts are big and sticky, but budgets move slowly. Commercial customers can expand fast once one deployment pays off. That speeds growth but adds exposure to corporate spending cycles.

Profit outran sales because most of Palantir's costs don't rise with revenue. Operating expenses grew about 46% while revenue nearly doubled. Software costs little to deliver once it's built, so most of each new dollar falls to profit.

The soft spot is new business. Palantir closed $2.92 billion in total contract value, up just 6% from a year ago. Revenue is recognized from contracts already signed. When signings grow far slower than sales, the company works through its backlog faster than it refills it. Big deals are lumpy, so one soft quarter isn't a trend yet.

The key number is U.S. commercial remaining deal value, which rose just 4% from last quarter while U.S. commercial revenue rose 29%. If that backlog doesn't speed up, today's growth rate will be hard to hold.

AI models can help users sort through mountains of files, generate videos that have Hollywood studios worried, and create everything from websites and businesses to custom video games. With what’s called vibe coding, ordinary people can build playable video games in minutes using simple text prompts in popular AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

But the AI company Anthropic appears to be drawing a line in the sand about what kinds of games its AI model Claude can make. If a Claude user is trying to recreate someone else’s intellectual property, the AI tool will decline to build it.

That’s according to Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic who posted on X. He was responding to concerns that Anthropic had changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games, which could violate copyright rules and the company’s usage policy.

“Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working,” Osmani said. “We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to…

He offered to review cases where amateur game developers believe Claude wrongly refused their requests.

A representative for Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic’s stance, as expressed by Osmani, acknowledges that using AI to try to clone a video game, even a simple one, could constitute intellectual property infringement, an issue that predates the rise of AI tools like Claude.

Even with the change, Claude will still generate video games that resemble popular hits from the past few decades. A CNET request to build a game “that resembled Breakout but with the word Claude on each brick” yielded a playable web version of the arcade classic, but not one that any video game fan would mistake for the original.

The same thing happened after Flappy Bird became a hit in 2014, spawning a wave of copycat games in app stores. Copyright infringement of games is complicated, said David Kocan, an intellectual property lawyer at Nixon Peabody who co-leads the firm’s esports and gaming team.

“This is something courts have wrestled with long before AI came along,” Kocan said. “The basic distinction has always been that copyright protects a game’s original creative expression, but generally not its underlying ideas, rules, or gameplay mechanics. Copyright protects the game you created, not the genre you helped popularize.”

You can’t copyright the concept of, say, a battle royal game or a side-scrolling platformer, which is why when a new type of game emerges as a hit, you’ll see many similar games.

“That distinction may sound straightforward in theory, but in practice, the line between borrowing an idea and copying someone’s creative expression can be blurry,” Kocan said. “That’s particularly true in gaming, where so much of the experience combines functional mechanics with creative expression.”

RTB Ruhan, founder and CEO of Null Station, an animation and video game art studio, said that AI has made it”fast and cheap” to cross the line into infringement, allowing people with no art or design skills to clone a popular game. But that doesn’t mean someone can publish or sell a cloned game without running into trouble.

“‘(Claiming) AI made it’ won’t protect them,” Ruhan said.

“Remove the title and logo and ask whether a player could still tell the two games apart,” Ruhan said. “If they can’t, you’ve crossed the line.”

Legal experts CNET spoke with said there are no laws requiring AI companies to outlaw game clones on their tools. But adding those guardrails could prevent trouble down the road, said Eric Blatt, a corporate, securities and intellectual property lawyer at Scale and a former examiner at the US Patent and Trademark Office.

“Anthropic is prudent to tap the brakes here,” Blatt said. “If Claude — Anthropic-owned software operating on Anthropic servers — receives an instruction to copy a game, and if Claude then copies the game, there is a facially plausible argument that Anthropic performed the copying. The chat logs would be a gold mine for the plaintiff’s counsel.”

Blatt said that litigation hasn’t kept pace with AI’s growth, but he thinks lawsuits could quickly follow if a rebuilt game made with AI directly threatens a company’s business model.

But some of those attempts could be stopped before they start if AI models refuse to make exact copies.

“Ultimately, copyright law draws the legal boundaries,” Kocan said. “But AI companies have to decide where they’re comfortable drawing their own. And those aren’t necessarily going to be the same thing.”

#3124. Amazon vs. Alibaba: Two E-Commerce Giants, a Big Valuation Gap, but Which Offers More Upside in 2027?

Amazon and Alibaba are investing heavily in the future of e-commerce and artificial intelligence, but a substantial valuation gap could make one the more attractive opportunity heading into 2027.

Can Western dominance in cloud and commerce outperform Eastern scale and a cheaper valuation? Choosing between Amazon.com (AMZN +2.20%) and Alibaba (BABA +3.53%) requires weighing domestic growth against international expansion.

Amazon focuses on logistics and cloud infrastructure to serve global consumers and enterprises. Alibaba leverages its vast ecosystem in China and emerging markets to facilitate trade and cloud services. Investors often compare them as the primary titans of their respective regions, each offering unique paths to long-term growth.

Amazon operates a massive logistics network and online marketplace, serving millions of global consumers through its dominance among retail stocks and cloud services. Its revenue comes from online retail, third-party seller services, advertising, cloud infrastructure, and Prime subscriptions, providing several sources of growth across consumer and enterprise markets.

In FY 2025, Amazon generated $716.9 billion in revenue, an increase of 12.4% year over year. Net income reached $77.7 billion, resulting in a profit margin of approximately 10.8%. Growth was supported by its retail operations and Amazon Web Services (AWS), which reported a 20% increase in annual sales as demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure continued to expand.

Amazon ended 2025 with a current ratio of approximately 1.1x and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.4x when including lease liabilities. Free cash flow totaled $11.2 billion, down from $38.2 billion in 2024, as the company substantially increased capital spending on AI infrastructure. While these investments are weighing on near-term cash generation, they could strengthen Amazon's long-term position in cloud computing and artificial intelligence.

Alibaba operates one of China's largest e-commerce and cloud computing platforms, serving consumers and businesses through Taobao, Tmall, and Alibaba Cloud. The company also maintains a growing international presence through platforms such as AliExpress, Lazada, and Alibaba.com, providing exposure to online retail, digital services, and enterprise technology markets.

In FY 2026, Alibaba generated $148.4 billion in revenue, an increase of 2.7% year over year. However, excluding businesses sold during the year, revenue increased approximately 11%, reflecting stronger growth across its continuing operations. Net income reached $14.8 billion, down approximately 19% from the prior year, resulting in a profit margin of 10%. The results highlight Alibaba's continued business expansion alongside pressure on profitability.

Alibaba ended fiscal 2026 with a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.25x, excluding lease liabilities, and a current ratio of 1.3x. Free cash flow was negative $6.8 billion, compared with positive $10.7 billion the previous year, as the company significantly increased investments in AI and cloud computing infrastructure. While these expenditures could support future growth, they have placed considerable pressure on near-term cash generation.

Alibaba operates in a complex regulatory environment that impacts its core e-commerce and cloud computing segments. The company must navigate intense competition from domestic rivals and shifting consumer habits within the Chinese market. Furthermore, geopolitical tensions and changes in international trade policy can affect its ability to expand successfully into other global markets over the next few years.

Alibaba appears cheaper, carrying a lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Alibaba looks particularly attractive from a valuation standpoint. Trading at 14.8 times forward earnings and 1.6 times sales, the company is considerably cheaper than Amazon, which trades at 18.7 times forward earnings and 3.3 times sales. Alibaba also has significant growth potential as it expands its cloud computing business and invests heavily in artificial intelligence infrastructure. However, intense competition in China, regulatory uncertainty, and pressure on profitability remain important considerations.

Amazon commands a premium, but that valuation appears justified by its stronger financial performance. Revenue increased 12.4% in 2025, compared with Alibaba's 2.7% growth, while AWS continues to benefit from accelerating demand for cloud computing and AI services. Both companies are spending heavily on infrastructure, but Amazon's stronger revenue momentum and more diversified business provide greater confidence in its ability to generate long-term returns.

For investors heading into 2027, Amazon looks like the better buy. Alibaba offers an appealing valuation and potentially greater upside if its growth accelerates, but Amazon's established competitive advantages, stronger earnings momentum, and exposure to the AI investment cycle make it the more compelling holding.

#3121. Vertex Spends Its CF Growth on New Launches: Rapid Earnings Reaction

Vertex's cystic fibrosis business is still growing, but the company is pouring those gains into new franchises. Here's what the third quarter shows about the cost of building its next act.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX -1.02%) grew third-quarter revenue 12% to $3.44 billion, as patients kept moving to its newer cystic fibrosis (CF) drug, Alyftrek. Shares rose about 1.5% in early after-hours trading. Adjusted profit was flat, though, because Vertex is spending its CF gains on new launches and the Crinetics deal. Profit will likely trail sales until those bets pay off.

Alyftrek is now replacing Trikafta, not just adding to it. Trikafta sales fell 8% as patients switched to a drug they take once a day instead of twice. With higher net prices on top, CF still grew. It's a steady engine, and it's paying for everything else.

Spending is soaking up the growth. Adjusted operating income rose only 2%. Vertex is building a kidney-drug sales team before it has a drug to sell, absorbing Crinetics, and still pushing Journavx. Launch costs land before launch revenue does. The steeper GAAP drop came mostly from one-time Crinetics deal costs, not taxes, since the GAAP tax rate didn't change.

Don't read much into the higher revenue forecast. The $50 million bump at the midpoint is about what newly acquired Palsonify is expected to add. Spending guidance went up too, and Vertex now carries debt from the deal.

Watch the FDA's Nov. 30 decision on povetacicept for IgA nephropathy, since Vertex is already spending to launch it. Interim data on VX-670 in myotonic dystrophy is also due by year-end.

#3119. Fabrinet's 51% Growth Comes at a Cash Cost: Rapid Earnings Reaction

Fabrinet's optical manufacturing business is growing fast. This quarter shows what that growth costs in cash and taxes, and what investors should track next.

Fabrinet (FN -3.85%) grew revenue 51% to about $1.47 billion in its fiscal first quarter, above the top of its own guidance range. Shares rose about 10% in after-hours trading. The demand is real, but this growth phase is eating cash. Fabrinet built inventory and factory capacity so fast that free cash flow turned negative and it took on debt.

Costs didn't cause the gap between sales growth and GAAP profit growth. Operating income grew faster than sales. Taxes and a write-down did the damage. Fabrinet booked a charge for the new global minimum tax and a loss on a private stake, then left both out of adjusted EPS. The write-down may be a one-off, but the tax isn't. Second-quarter guidance excludes another $0.60 per share for it, so GAAP earnings are the better guide to what owners keep.

The cash drain is the price of scaling. A contract manufacturer buys parts and builds capacity before customers pay. Capital spending more than tripled to about $159 million, while inventory and receivables swelled. Fabrinet sold short-term investments and drew loans that weren't on its balance sheet in June to cover the gap.

Guidance says the ramp isn't slowing. Management expects second-quarter revenue of $1.6 billion to $1.65 billion, up from this quarter. If that holds, the spending is buying real growth, not idle capacity.

Watch whether operating cash flow recovers next quarter as new programs ship and customers pay. Also watch whether Fabrinet keeps buying back stock while free cash flow stays negative.

#3117. Acadia Realty: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Direct-to-consumer retailers are competing fiercely for Acadia's urban storefronts, a structural tailwind that justifies the company's disciplined acquisition strategy.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 2, 2026, Acadia Realty (AKR +1.89%) announced elevated same-property net operating income growth, which measures profitability from established real estate locations, driven by street retail performance. For long-term investors, the company's focus on high-density urban corridors creates a structural advantage as street leases adjust to market prices faster than suburban properties. Three things management said stand out.

Traditional leases tie landlords to fixed renewal options for decades, limiting rent growth during inflationary periods. Fair market value resets allow Acadia Realty to mark rents to prevailing rates every five years, capturing rapid market price increases across its urban storefronts.

Apparel and retail brands are shifting away from department stores to open direct-to-consumer (DTC) storefronts. This expansion creates intense tenant competition for prime street space, keeping store sales high while pushing rental rates higher.

The company acquired $150 million of street retail assets in the quarter, bringing its total to $350 million for the year. By purchasing properties with near-term lease-up potential in top corridors, management targets cash yields exceeding 7% upon stabilization.

Street leasing momentum is converting directly into contracted future revenue through signed but not yet open leases.

Clustered street ownership gives the company pricing discipline and direct tenant relationships across key urban markets.

#3116. As Fed Holds Steady, Are 7.5% Mortgage Rates Still Possible?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The Fed voted to hold rates steady, but mortgage rates still have room to grow.

On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve announced that central bankers would leave the federal funds rate unchanged. Since this was in line with market expectations, mortgage rates shouldn’t have much of a reaction — yet.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage slid 10 basis points to 7.17% APR in the week ending Oct. 28, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Central bankers have twin goals when setting monetary policy: Getting inflation as close to 2% as possible, and maintaining maximum employment. When inflation gets too high, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which causes consumer borrowing rates (like mortgage rates) to rise as well. When unemployment gets too high, they can lower the federal funds rate to make it cheaper for businesses to access credit and hire more employees.

Since the latest jobs report showed that employment was relatively steady last month, that leaves inflation as the hot topic.

Despite Fed Chair Kevin Warsh holding true to his signature tight-lipped style in the weeks leading up to the meeting — and despite September’s preliminary inflation numbers running high so far — futures traders were largely confident that the Fed would keep the federal funds rate as is this week after last month’s hike.

Not necessarily. Mortgage rates could be completely different tomorrow.

In fact, we’ll probably see rates shift in response to the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, or PCE, which is set to be released on Thursday, Oct. 29. This is the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. Central bankers didn’t have this data during voting, which may be one reason they decided against adjusting the federal funds rate again quite yet.

If this week’s PCE data shows inflation rising, mortgage rates will probably go up over the next few weeks as lenders look to protect their investment against a weakening dollar. Rising inflation also bolsters the case for a rate hike at the central bankers’ next meeting; according to the futures traders behind CME FedWatch, there’s a very good chance that the Fed will announce an increase on Dec. 9.

And there is reason to think that PCE will show growing inflation. September’s monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures changes in prices of everyday goods and services, was released on Oct. 14 and showed annual inflation rising to 3.7%.

Of course, mortgage rates respond to all sorts of things. Oil prices, the bond market, global and national events — any number of hard-to-predict happenings could swing rates in the coming days and weeks. But if market analysts dig their heels into the idea of a December rate hike from the Fed, you should probably prepare for higher mortgage rates in November.

So far, 30-year mortgage rates are averaging 7.3% for October, compared with September’s average of 6.98%. On this trajectory, it’s conceivable that we could see rates hit 7.5% this year — a monthly average we haven’t seen since October 2023.

If and when the Fed does raise the federal funds rate again, it will be meant as a temporary treatment for overheated inflation.

Think of it as bitter medicine: It might be tough to swallow, but getting inflation under control actually paves the way for lower rates down the line. Moderating inflation could also lead to lower prices on essential goods that have been eating away at the prospective home buyer’s wallet, freeing up more cash for your monthly mortgage payment.
